 CRISPR  Screens to Discover Potential Therapeutic Targets CRISPR‐based functional genomic screens have revolutionized cancer research by enabling systematic interrogation of gene function at scale, thereby facilitating the discovery of novel drug targets and therapeutic vulnerabilities [ 106 ,  107 ]. Genome‐wide or focused CRISPRko, CRISPRi, and CRISPRa screens have been employed to identify genes essential for cancer cell survival, proliferation, metastasis, and drug resistance across a range of tumor types [ 108 ]. These unbiased approaches allow researchers to define context‐specific dependencies that are not evident from mutational data alone, particularly in genetically complex or heterogeneous cancers [ 41 ,  109 ]. One landmark example is the genome‐scale CRISPRko screens performed across hundreds of cancer cell lines to generate a comprehensive Cancer Dependency Map [ 110 ]. This revealed lineage‐specific essential genes and potential drug targets such as  BCL2L1  in hematologic malignancies and  WRN  in microsatellite instability‐high (MSI‐H) cancers [ 110 ]. These findings not only highlighted tumor‐selective vulnerabilities, such as dependencies on DNA damage response genes (e.g.,  BRCA1/2 ) or epigenetic regulators (e.g.,  EZH2 ), but also informed targeted drug development strategies, including  PARP  inhibitors for  BRCA ‐mutant tumors and  EZH2  inhibitors for cancers with dysregulated epigenetic programs [ 111 ,  112 ]. CRISPR screens have also been instrumental in identifying synthetic lethal interactions, reflecting the two‐hit hypothesis, where the loss of a second gene is lethal only in the context of a pre‐existing cancer‐specific alteration [ 113 ]. In vivo CRISPR screens conducted in a mouse melanoma model identified  Ptpn2  as a negative regulator of interferon‐γ signaling. The loss of  Ptpn2  enhanced the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade therapy by promoting tumor‐intrinsic interferon‐γ responses, revealing a potential combinatorial immunotherapy target [ 114 ]. This also represents a form of synthetic lethality, as tumor cells remain viable with either  Ptpn2  expression or immune checkpoint blockade alone, but the combination selectively induces tumor cell death by sensitizing tumors to immune‐mediated killing [ 115 ,  116 ]. Similarly, CRISPR screens conducted in  BRCA1/2 ‐deficient cells identified  POLQ  as a synthetic lethal partner, paving the way for targeted therapies exploiting homologous recombination deficiencies [ 117 ].  POLQ  inhibition selectively kills homologous recombination‐deficient tumor cells, paving the way for targeted therapies in  BRCA ‐mutant cancers and overcoming  PARP  inhibitor resistance [ 118 ,  119 ,  120 ]. Beyond gene knockouts, CRISPRi/a screens have expanded the search for non‐mutated but dysregulated genes involved in oncogenesis or drug resistance. CRISPRi screening targeting chromatin modifiers identified epigenetic regulators that sensitize glioblastoma cells to  BET  inhibitors [ 121 ]. Additionally, combination screens pairing CRISPR alterations with small‐molecule treatments (e.g., chemotherapies, kinase inhibitors, or immune modulators) have uncovered drug‐gene interactions critical for therapeutic response. An example of this is a study where CRISPR‐based chemogenomic screens were used to identify genes involved in the DNA damage response that, when lost, sensitized cancer cells to ATR inhibitors [ 122 ]. Together, these studies exemplify the transformative role of CRISPR screening in defining the functional landscape of the cancer genome, prioritizing drug targets, and enabling the rational design of genotype‐directed therapies [ 80 ,  123 ]. As screening platforms expand to incorporate PDOs, immune‐competent models, and single‐cell culture, CRISPR screens are poised to play an increasingly central role in precision oncology [ 72 ,  124 ]. Across studies, a consistent finding is that PDO‐based CRISPR screens are particularly effective at uncovering context‐dependent genetic dependencies that may not be apparent from genomic profiling alone. Multiple investigations have identified vulnerabilities linked to specific mutational backgrounds, suggesting that functional dependencies are often shaped by tumor lineage, cellular state, and microenvironmental influences rather than genotype alone. While these findings collectively support the use of PDOs as biologically relevant screening platforms, differences in organoid culture conditions, screening scale, and analytical approaches complicate direct comparison between studies. Furthermore, many reported dependencies have been validated only in limited cohorts, making it difficult to determine whether they represent broadly applicable therapeutic targets or highly context‐specific vulnerabilities. Future studies involving larger multi‐centre organoid collections and standardized screening pipelines will be necessary to establish the reproducibility and clinical significance of these findings. 3.2 Using  CRISPR  Screens to Uncover Mechanisms of Drug Resistance By systematically perturbing genes across the genome, CRISPRko, CRISPRi, and CRISPRa platforms allow for unbiased identification of genes that modulate drug sensitivity or drive resistance [ 125 ]. These screens have revealed both well‐characterized and novel resistance mechanisms, informing the development of combination therapies and predictive biomarkers. The utility of genome‐wide CRISPRko screens was demonstrated by identifying  NF1  as a key modulator of resistance to vemurafenib in  BRAF ‐mutant melanoma cells, highlighting a compensatory  MAPK  signaling pathway [ 126 ]. Similarly, CRISPRko screens uncovered  MED12  loss as a broad driver of resistance to multiple tyrosine kinase inhibitors through activation of  TGF‐β  signaling, suggesting a convergent resistance mechanism with therapeutic implications [ 127 ]. CRISPRi screens have proven particularly valuable in identifying resistance‐associated genes that are not essential for cell viability but whose transcriptional suppression confers survival advantages under drug pressure. CRISPRi employed to screen non‐essential genes in  KRAS ‐mutant lung cancer cells treated with  MEK  inhibitors identified the transcriptional regulator  SPRED2  as a modulator of drug response via  MAPK  feedback reactivation [ 128 ]. Moreover, CRISPRa approaches have been used to model gain‐of‐function resistance mechanisms. A CRISPRa screen identified that the overexpression of  ABCB1 , a multidrug efflux transporter, functions as a driver of resistance to a range of chemotherapeutics, validating the role of transcriptional activation in acquired resistance [ 129 ]. These strategies have also been applied to physiologically relevant models, including PDOs and in vivo tumors, where they have helped identify resistance‐associated genes and reveal new therapeutic targets relevant to precision oncology [ 49 ,  114 ]. For instance, organoid‐based CRISPR perturbations have been applied to identify synthetic lethal interactions and to prioritize candidate genes for targeted therapies, highlighting their potential in preclinical drug development [ 130 ,  131 ,  132 ]. Furthermore, integrating CRISPR screens with single‐cell RNA sequencing in PDOs has provided insights into tumor heterogeneity and resistance mechanisms, as demonstrated in studies exploring gene–environment interactions within the tumor microenvironment [ 72 ]. Collectively, these studies demonstrate the power of CRISPR screens in organoid systems to map the complex genetic architecture of drug resistance—including loss‐of‐function and gain‐of‐function adaptations, feedback signaling loops, and epigenetic regulation [ 133 ,  134 ,  135 ]. Although the specific resistance mechanisms identified differ between tumor types and therapeutic agents, a common theme emerging across studies is that resistance rarely arises from a single genetic event. Instead, CRISPR‐based screens consistently reveal complex interactions between genetic alterations, transcriptional programs, and adaptive cellular states. Several studies have demonstrated the importance of tumor heterogeneity in shaping therapeutic response, while others have highlighted the contribution of non‐genetic mechanisms such as cellular plasticity. Differences in reported resistance pathways likely reflect variations in tumor biology, treatment context, and screening methodology rather than contradictory findings. Collectively, the evidence suggests that PDO‐based CRISPR screens provide a more comprehensive representation of resistance evolution than conventional 2D systems, although further integration with longitudinal patient data will be required to establish the clinical relevance of many proposed resistance mechanisms. 3.3 Study Tumor Heterogeneity and Evolution Through  CRISPR  Screens Tumor heterogeneity and clonal evolution represent major barriers to effective cancer therapy, contributing to treatment resistance, disease progression, and recurrence [ 136 ,  137 ,  138 ]. CRISPR‐based screening approaches have emerged as powerful tools for dissecting the functional underpinnings of intra‐tumoral heterogeneity and tracking clonal dynamics in complex cancer models such as PDOs. By enabling the parallel interrogation of gene function across diverse subpopulations, CRISPR screens can reveal how genetic and non‐genetic variations influence therapy response and lineage trajectories within tumors [ 72 ,  106 ]. For example, the use of multiplexed CRISPR screening with molecular barcoding to track the fate of edited clones in a pooled format lays the groundwork for lineage‐tracing studies in heterogeneous tumor populations [ 139 ,  140 ]. Combining CRISPR screening with single‐cell RNA sequencing (Perturb‐seq) in PDOs enables mapping of how genetic perturbations reshape transcriptional programs at the single‐cell level. This approach has revealed context‐dependent effects of oncogenes and tumor suppressors across cellular subtypes, uncovering mechanisms of inter‐tumoral heterogeneity and potential determinants of therapy response [ 141 ,  142 ]. Moreover, lineage tracing tools based on CRISPR barcoding, such as CRISPR‐induced lineage tracing with expressed barcodes (e.g., LINNAEUS and CARLIN systems), have been adapted to PDO platforms to study tumor evolution over time [ 143 ,  144 ,  145 ]. Such approaches allow for the reconstruction of phylogenetic trees and identification of evolutionary bottlenecks, enabling direct observation of clonal competition and adaptation in a controlled ex vivo environment [ 146 ,  147 ,  148 ]. As these technologies are integrated with spatial transcriptomics and in vivo PDO engraftment models, CRISPR screening is poised to offer unprecedented insights into the rules governing tumor heterogeneity, clonal selection, and resistance evolution [ 149 ]. The studies discussed in this section collectively demonstrate that tumor heterogeneity is not merely a source of experimental variability but a fundamental determinant of screening outcomes. While some investigations have focused on genetic diversity as the primary driver of heterogeneity, others have emphasized the importance of transcriptional plasticity and dynamic cell‐state transitions. sources.title: Microsatellite Instable Cancer Cells Acquire On-target Resistance Mutations to WRN Helicase Inhibitors.
sources.abstract: The Werner syndrome helicase (WRN) is a promising target for cancers with microsatellite instability (MSI), leading to the initiation of at least five phase I clinical trials. Acquired resistance is a substantial obstacle to obtaining lasting benefits from targeted therapies in oncology and may be particularly acute in the setting of mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) tumors, which can sample increased fitness landscapes owing to a higher mutational burden. In this study, we characterized resistance mechanisms using the clinical candidate HRO761 and two novel inhibitors in MSI cell lines and xenograft models. We observed the rapid emergence of resistance both in vitro and in vivo, with sequencing revealing clustered mutations within the WRN helicase domain. Computational structural analyses indicated that these mutations either directly interfere with inhibitor binding or alter the protein conformation required for inhibitor engagement. Notably, although most mutations conferred broad resistance across all three compounds, we identified specific alterations (L528S, C727R, and F730L) that exhibited selectivity between chemical scaffolds. This chemotype-specific resistance profile suggests opportunities for developing next-generation inhibitors that retain activity against resistant variants and for implementing rational treatment strategies with existing inhibitors. Overall, our findings demonstrate that on-target resistance to WRN inhibitors emerges rapidly in dMMR backgrounds but also highlight potential approaches to overcome resistance, supporting the continued development of WRN-targeted therapies for MSI cancers.
sources.full_text_excerpt: Introduction Microsatellite instability (MSI) arising from deficient DNA mismatch repair (dMMR) is a feature of several cancer types, especially colorectal and endometrial cancers ( 1 ). MSI-high (MSI-H)/dMMR status has been approved as a predictive biomarker for immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) response, with pembrolizumab approved for first-line treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer and as a tumor-agnostic therapy for MSI-H/dMMR solid tumors that are metastatic or unresectable after failure of prior treatment. Despite these approvals, clinical trials demonstrate that approximately 30% of patients with MSI-H metastatic colorectal cancer and up to 50% of patients with various MSI-H solid tumors display innate resistance to ICI therapy, highlighting the need for additional therapeutic approaches specifically for MSI tumors ( 2 ,  3 ). Given the success of PARP inhibitors in treating  BRCA 1/2-mutated cancers, significant effort has been made to identify additional synthetic lethal relationships to guide drug discovery through large-scale screening efforts ( 4 – 6 ). The results of these screens revealed a previously unobserved synthetic lethal relationship between genetic dependency on Werner syndrome helicase (WRN) and MSI ( 6 – 8 ). WRN is a member of the RecQ helicase family and plays an important role during replication stress and double-strand break repair to preserve genomic integrity ( 9 ). MSI cancers frequently accumulate expanded (TA) dinucleotide repeats that can form a DNA cruciform secondary structure, which requires WRN helicase for resolution. Genetic knockdown of  WRN  in cell lines and organoids harboring these expanded TA repeats leads to replication fork stalling and MUS81/SLX4-induced DNA cleavage at sites of TA repeat expansions, ultimately leading to apoptosis or senescence ( 6 ,  10 ). Based on the promising genetic data of this synthetic lethal relationship, several groups have developed potent, specific small-molecule inhibitors of WRN helicase activity with selective efficacy in MSI but not microsatellite stable cellular and patient-derived xenograft models. Five of these programs are in phase I clinical trials at the time of writing ( NCT05838768 ,  NCT06004245 ,  NCT06710847 ,  NCT06898450 ,  NCT06974110 ; refs.  11 – 14 ). Though these inhibitors show strong cellular and  in vivo  responses initially ( 13 ), the issue of acquired resistance to these inhibitors has not been explored. Acquired resistance may be of particular concern in the context of MSI, as these cancers, by definition, acquire mutations easily. Additionally, many WRN inhibitors being developed are allosteric inhibitors, which are susceptible to several distinct resistance mechanisms ( 15 ). To investigate potential resistance mechanisms to WRN-directed therapeutics, we utilized two structurally distinct WRN helicase inhibitors from our drug discovery program. By evaluating these compounds in cellular MSI models, we identified three acquired point mutations that confer resistance to WRN inhibition. Additionally, we drove resistance to Novartis’ clinical candidate HRO761 ( NCT05838768 ) and identified seven acquired resistance mutations  in vivo  and four  in vitro . Although most mutations conveyed similar levels of resistance to all three compounds, three were specific to different chemotypes despite the similarity in binding site and mechanism of action of all three inhibitors. Our findings highlight the potential for WRN-directed therapeutics to lead to acquired resistance in patients and suggest that combination therapy may be necessary for durable therapeutic success. Additionally, our findings provide direction for next-generation WRN inhibitors, which could be designed to avoid these resistance mechanisms or specifically target tumors resistant to first-generation WRN inhibitors. Materials and Methods Cell culture The following cell lines were procured from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) in the indicated year: DLD-1 (2015, RRID:CVCL_0248), HCT116 (2017, RRID:CVCL_0291), RKO (2018, RRID:CVCL_0504), RL95-2 (2020, RRID:CVCL_0505), LS411N (2018, RRID:CVCL_1385), LS180 (2016, RRID:CVCL_0397), SW620 (2015, RRID:CVCL_0547), and SW48 (2017, RRID:CVCL_1724). Ishikawa cells (2014, RRID:CVCL_2529) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. HEC-6 cells were purchased from JCRB Cell Bank (2017, RRID:CVCL_2931). DLD-1, HCT116, LS411N, SW48, and Ishikawa cell lines were grown in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 10% FBS, GlutaMAX, sodium pyruvate, and 100 μg/mL Normocin (InvivoGen, #ant-nr-2) or 1% penicillin/streptomycin at 37°C and 5% CO 2 . RL95-2 cells were grown in DMEM:F12 supplemented with 10% FBS, 100 μg/mL Normocin (InvivoGen, #ant-nr-2), and 0.005 mg/mL insulin. LS180 cells were grown in Eagle Minimum Essential Medium (EMEM) supplemented with 10% FBS and 100 μg/mL Normocin (InvivoGen, #ant-nr-2). SW620 cells were grown in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 100 μg/mL Normocin (InvivoGen, #ant-nr-2). HEC-6 cells were grown in EMEM supplemented with 15% FBS and 100 μg/mL Normocin (InvivoGen, #ant-nr-2). Cells were tested for the presence of mycoplasma monthly using MycoAlert PLUS (Lonza, #LT07-710). Cells were maintained at low passages after purchase, so authentication was not performed. AC1 and AC2 cell viability HCT116, RKO, DLD1 (500 cells), or SW48 (1,500 cells) were seeded in 384-well plates and allowed to adhere overnight. Cells were treated with compound at a top dose of 20 μmol/L, with 1:3 serial dilutions, in a 10-pt dose response. After 5 days, cells were quantitated by the CyQUANT GR Cell Proliferation Assay (Molecular Probes) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. EC 50  and SD values were calculated by normalizing counts to the DMSO control and represent the average of ≥2 biological replicates ( Fig. 1D ). Figure 1. A,  Structures of Calico/AbbVie series 1 inhibitor AC1 (left) and series 2 inhibitor AC2 (right) used for resistance experiments. After 72 hours at 37°C, viability was measured using CellTiter-Glo (Promega, #G7573) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Viability was normalized to DMSO control wells and represents the average of three technical replicates on each plate and two biological replicates (Supplementary Fig. S1D). γH2AX induction RKO, DLD-1, SW48, HCT116, and Ishikawa cells were plated in collagen-coated, black 96-well plates and allowed to adhere overnight. Cells were treated with the compound in 1:2 serial dilutions for 3 days. Cells were fixed in 2% formaldehyde and permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X. A blank surface had an immobilized biotin-Tris NTA-neutravidin surface in the reference flow cell and was used as a reference surface during binding assays. Compounds were assayed using single-cycle kinetics mode as provided by the Biacore T200 control software. The compounds were diluted in the running buffer and injected in a series of increasing concentrations for a contact time of 65 seconds each, and dissociation was monitored for up to 500 seconds. Ethics statement AbbVie is committed to ensuring the humane care and use of laboratory animals in the company’s research and development programs. Our programs exceed regulatory agency standards, and we are committed to the internationally accepted principles of refinement, reduction, and replacement. All animal studies were reviewed and approved by AbbVie’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee or Oversight Body (in accordance with national regulations). Animal studies were conducted under an Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care International–accredited program, in which veterinary care and oversight were provided to ensure optimal animal care. All studies presented here used female CB17-SCID (6–8 weeks of age upon arrival) mice purchased from Charles River Laboratories. Animals were allowed to acclimate to the facility for at least 1 week prior to the initiation of the experiments. The maximum tumor volume endpoint defined per the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee protocol was 2,000 mm 3  and was calculated by applying the following equation: volume = (length × width 2 )/2. Any individual animal with a tumor measurement greater than 2,000 mm 3  or with body weight loss (from predosing baseline) greater than or equal to 20% was removed from the study and humanely euthanized. HRO761 efficacy in SW48 xenograft model SW48 cells were purchased from the ATCC and were cultured in DMEM (Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS. Mice were inoculated in the lower right hind flank with 5 × 10 6  cells suspended in a 1:1 mixture of Spinner Minimum Essential Medium (Gibco) and Matrigel (Corning). Tumor size was measured 2 to 3 times per week using electronic calipers. Body weight was also collected once weekly to monitor for body weight changes due to treatment. Following subcutaneous SW48 cell inoculation, mice were randomized into dosing groups with an average predosing tumor size of approximately 185 mm 3 . The next day, mice began their dosing regimen and were dosed by oral gavage with vehicle, 60 mg/kg HRO761, 120 mg/kg HRO761, or 200 mg/kg HRO761 once a day for 14 consecutive days. HRO761 was prepared for  in vivo  administration in 10% hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin, with a final pH of 7.4 (±0.2). The maximal tumor growth inhibition (TGI Max ) was calculated using the following formula: TGI = 100 − [(ΔT/ΔC) × 100], where ΔT or ΔC is the volume change from randomization of treated and vehicle-treated tumors. HRO761 rechallenge On day 48 after randomization, 10 mice (representative of all three initial HRO761 dosing groups) were rerandomized into two new treatment groups (vehicle and 120 mg/kg HRO761) with an average tumor volume of 240 to 260 mm 3 . Treatment by oral gavage began the following day, and mice received a total of nine daily doses prior to humane euthanasia and harvest. Tumors were excised and immediately flash-frozen for subsequent WES analysis. Tumor dissociation for cell line generation Excised tumor tissue was removed and processed utilizing sterile technique to minimize the introduction of contaminants to dissociated tumor tissue. Briefly, tumor tissue was removed and forced through a sterile metal sieve while rinsing with cold RPMI to collect a tumor cell suspension devoid of connective or other fibrous tissue. Collected cells were then transferred into T175 flasks with RPMI containing 10% FBS and 1× penicillin-streptomycin antibiotics (Gibco). Cells remained in the antibiotic media for three consecutive passages, and antibiotics were removed once no visible contaminants remained. To further confirm the cells were clean, they were sent to a commercial diagnostic lab for sterility and murine pathogen screening prior to further use. In addition, the same commercial vendor also confirmed via STR profiling that the newly cultured cells were of the parental SW48 origin. HRO761 efficacy in the HRO761-resistant SW48 xenograft model HRO761-resistant cells dissociated from treated SW48 tumors were cultured in DMEM (Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS. Mice were inoculated in the lower right hind flank with 5 × 10 6  cells suspended in a 1:1 mixture of SMEM (Gibco) and Matrigel (Corning). Following subcutaneous cell inoculation, mice were randomized into dosing groups with an average predosing tumor size of approximately 170 mm 3 . The next day, mice began their dosing regimen and were dosed by oral gavage with either vehicle or 120 mg/kg HRO761 once a day for 14 consecutive days. Data (tumor growth and body weight) were collected and presented (TGI Max ) as previously described. Whole-exome sequencing A chunk of frozen tumor was excised, and then genomic DNA was extracted using a QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (QIAGEN, # 56304). This genomic DNA was sent to Azenta Life Sciences, where whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed. WES data analysis The WES fastq files were downloaded from the Azenta server and aligned to the hg38 genome using DragMap 1.2.1 with default parameters. The aligned BAM files were indexed and sorted using Samtools 1.17 and marked for duplicates using the Picard 3.0.0 MarkDuplicates command. Duplicate-marked sorted BAM files were then used to specifically examine the WRN locus by generating wig files representing base coverage within a 100 base pair window surrounding WRN using the IGVTools 2.16.2 count command. The resulting wig files were processed by a custom Python script to identify variants. The workflow filtered for positions with >20 read depth, calculated the most prevalent nonreference allele at each position, and retained variants with allele frequency ≥10%. Selected variants were then annotated for coding impact using RefSeq transcript information. Variants resulting in protein-coding changes that were not common to all samples were considered potential resistance mechanisms. Molecular docking We performed molecular docking of AC2 with the WRN helicase region using a crystal structure of WRN residues 526 to 946, cocrystallized with a similar inhibitor (with a Tanimoto similarity of 0.821, Shape Tanimoto similarity of 0.720, and MACCS Tanimoto of 0.973 obtained from RDKit similarity search ( 16 ). The crystal structure was resolved at a resolution of 1.77 Å, sufficient to model crystallographic water molecules within the inhibitor binding site. These water molecules were retained for docking calculations, as they contributed to key protein–ligand interactions. Prior to docking, the WRN crystal structure was prepared using the Molecular Operating Environment (MOE) QuickPrep module ( 17 ). Preparation included adjustment of protonation states at pH 7.0, addition of hydrogens, and energy minimization using the AMBER10:EHT force field. During minimization, default tether restraints were applied to backbone atoms, and convergence was defined by an root mean square gradient threshold of 0.1 kcal·mol −1 ·Å −2 . Molecular docking of AC2 was then carried out using three docking protocols available in MOE: (i) general docking, (ii) template docking: similarity, and (iii) template docking: substructure. For the general docking protocol, we tested docking both with and without the crystallographic waters. Including water molecules yielded improved binding poses and more favorable docking scores. In general docking, initial ligand poses were generated using the MOE Triangular Matcher algorithm, producing 1,000 conformations based on shape complementarity. These were scored using the London dG scoring function, and the top 100 poses were retained. Final pose refinement was carried out using the rigid receptor method combined with the GBVI/WSA dG scoring function. The top-ranked binding poses from all three protocols were evaluated, and the best-scoring models were selected for further analysis. All docking studies were conducted using the MOE Dock module ( 17 ). The top docking poses of the WRN–AC2 complex were further refined by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Prior to simulations, each complex underwent a second round of structure preparation using MOE QuickPrep to ensure correct protonation and geometry. Each complex was solvated in a cubic water box of dimensions 10 × 10 × 10 nm 3  containing ∼30,000 explicit water molecules and counterions to neutralize the system and maintain a physiologic salt concentration of 150 mmol/L. MD simulations were performed using GROMACS 2023 ( 18 ) with the AMBER14SB force field ( 19 ) for the protein. Ligand parameters were generated using GAFF ( 20 ) via ANTECHAMBER ( 21 ) with partial charges taken directly from MOE to maintain consistency between docking and simulation stages. After energy minimization and equilibration, each system was simulated for ∼900 ns under periodic boundary conditions and the NPT ensemble. Trajectory analysis using VMD 1.9.4 ( 22 ) showed that the best pose from general docking of the WRN–AC2 complex remained stable throughout the simulation, with a protein–ligand complex root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 3.4 ± 0.5 Å and a ligand-only RMSD of 1.8 ± 0.4 Å relative to the initial structure. Following confirmation of the predicted AC2 binding site stability, we evaluated the impact of known resistance mutations in WRN on AC2 binding. For each mutant (C727R, F730L, G729D, I852F, and L737F), we started from the WT WRN–AC2 docking model. The AC2 ligand was removed, and point mutations were introduced using the MOE Protein Builder module. Local refinement around the mutation site was then performed to accommodate structural changes. Subsequently, the refined mutant WRN structures were used for docking AC2, using only the general docking protocol as it had demonstrated superior performance and stability in our initial tests. The best binding pose for each mutant was analyzed and reported. The WRN crystal structure (PDB 9OG3), cocrystallized with a chemically similar inhibitor (with a Tanimoto similarity of 0.717, Shape Tanimoto similarity of 0.703, and MACCS Tanimoto of 0.953 obtained from RDKit similarity search), was used to dock AC1. Crystallographic waters were retained, and the protein was prepared with MOE QuickPrep. We used three MOE protocols: general docking, template docking (similarity), and template docking (substructure). Calculations for AC1 were performed in the same manner as for AC2. Top-ranked poses from all protocols were evaluated, and the best-scoring pose is reported here. Results Characterization of AbbVie/Calico WRN helicase inhibitors Our endeavor to develop small-molecule inhibitors of WRN helicase activity from a DNA-encoded library screen resulted in two series of allosteric inhibitors called S1 ( 23 ) and S2 (discovery and optimization will be reported elsewhere). We selected inhibitors from each series with the most potent cellular activity to characterize (called AC1 and AC2). SPR was performed to measure the dissociation constants (KD) of AC1 and AC2 with purified WRN core helicase domain (human WRN residues 506–1,068), which were 2 and 54 nmol/L, respectively ( Fig. 1A ; Supplementary Fig. S1A). A biochemical DNA unwinding assay to determine the ability of these small molecules to inhibit WRN helicase activity measured the IC 50  of 9.5 nmol/L for AC1 and 15 nmol/L for AC2 ( Fig. 1A ; Supplementary Fig. S1B). A crystal structure of the S2 inhibitor (AC3, PDB xxx) with WRN (residues 526–946) was solved and revealed that this inhibitor causes a massive conformational change in the WRN helicase region that presumably renders it inactive. This mechanism is similar to other WRN inhibitors described in the literature, including our previously published S1 inhibitors ( Fig. 1B ; ref.  23 ). Using these crystal structures as templates, we performed molecular docking to model AC2 bound to WRN. The docking suggests that AC2 interacts with R854 through an ionic interaction. R854 is a key residue acting as the arginine finger in ATP binding ( 12 ), thereby blocking ATP access when engaged by AC2 ( Fig. 1C ). We next docked AC1 into WRN and observed that R854 and R857 engage AC1 tightly, suggesting that blocking these key residues contributes to WRN inhibition (Supplementary Fig. S1C). AbbVie/Calico WRN helicase inhibitors are synthetic lethal in MSI-H cells Next, we characterized the cellular response to AC1 and AC2 treatment using a panel of MSI-H cell lines. AC1 and AC2 treatment led to a significant loss of viability in all MSI-H lines tested except DLD-1, which is not genetically dependent on  WRN  or sensitive to Novartis’ clinical candidate HRO761 ( Fig. 1D ; Supplementary Fig. S1D; ref.  13 ). Additionally, these compounds induce DNA damage specifically in sensitive cell lines, consistent with previous observations that knockdown of  WRN  leads to DNA damage in MSI-H models ( Fig. 1E ; Supplementary Fig. S1E; refs.  6 – 8 ). Overall, AC1 and AC2 are potent allosteric inhibitors of WRN helicase activity that exhibit cellular efficacy. Treatment with WRN inhibitors selects for point mutations in the helicase domain that confer drug resistance Next, we wanted to demonstrate the on-target activity of our inhibitors and explore potential mechanisms of allosteric inhibitor resistance in the context of MSI. We grew HCT116 and SW48 cells in AC1- or AC2-containing media at the EC 90 , EC 90  × 1.5, and EC 90 /1.5 calculated for each cell line/inhibitor combination, alongside a DMSO control ( Fig. 2A ). Most inhibitor-treated cells died in 3 to 5 days, followed by the emergence of resistant colonies after an additional 2 to 4 weeks in drug culture. We PCR amplified the  WRN  helicase region (residues 485–911) of these resistant cell populations and performed Sanger sequencing on the PCR product. In HCT116 cells, all doses of AC1 resulted in a G729D mutation, and all doses of AC2 resulted in a deletion of D526_P530del. In SW48 cells, all doses of AC1 resulted in a deletion of D526_P530del, and all doses of AC2 resulted in an L528S mutation. All mutations were heterozygous. Figure 2. In subsequent experiments, the resistant HCT116 cell lines harboring a WRN G729D mutation treated with AC1 and AC2 demonstrated IC 50  increases of 23- and 11-fold, respectively, compared with the parental cell line ( Fig. 2B ; Supplementary Table S1). To confirm that these mutations were sufficient to drive inhibitor resistance, we used a DNA unwinding assay to measure helicase activity. We found that the IC 50  of both AC1 and AC2 was increased 9- and 13-fold against a G729D mutant protein compared with the WT control ( Fig. 2C ; Supplementary Table S1). Additionally, we measured the binding affinity of purified WRN G729D to our inhibitors and found a 10-fold (AC1) and 4-fold (AC2) decrease in binding affinity compared with WT WRN (Supplementary Fig. S2A; Supplementary Table S2). This suggests that a G729D mutation may convey resistance to our inhibitors by decreasing the accessibility of the binding site. To assess this hypothesis, we generated a structural model of the G729D WRN mutant. Starting from our WT docking model ( Fig. 1C ), we introduced the G729D mutant and allowed the local environment to relax using the MOE ( 17 ) Protein Builder module. We find that this mutation results in a new hydrogen bond between D729 and T573, which notably alters the AC2 pocket ( Fig. 2D ). Remarkably, this model produces a substantial shift of F730 into the inhibitor binding site (RMSD = 5.7 Å compared with WT), with the resulting movement likely causing a steric clash with AC2 and thereby preventing its binding. Molecular docking of AC2 to the G729D WRN confirmed this disruption, as the ligand was no longer able to adopt a WT-like binding pose [RMSD = 6.1 Å;  Fig. 2D  (right)]. Given that WRN G729D cells were resistant to AC1 and that the two inhibitors share a similar allosteric binding site, we hypothesize that AC1 would also exhibit a steric clash with F730. Altogether, these data suggest that a G729D mutation in WRN results in reduced binding of inhibitors and allows WRN to retain helicase activity in the presence of WRN inhibitors. Next, we assessed the resistance profile of WRN D526_P530del cells, which arose in AC2-challenged HCT116 cells and AC1-challenged SW48 cells. The WRN D526_P530del cell line was resistant to both inhibitors, and both inhibitors displayed reduced binding and inhibition of helicase activity to WRN D526_P530del compared with WT WRN ( Fig. 2E  and  F ; Supplementary Fig. S2B; Supplementary Tables S1 and S2). Through WES, we determined that this cell line acquired a point mutation at the splice acceptor site for exon 13, which led to the usage of the next possible “AG” splice site, resulting in a 15 bp deletion in exon 13 (Supplementary Fig. S2C). The WRN L528S mutation was observed in a pool of AC2-resistant SW48 cells, but these cells also had a G729D mutation at a lower allele frequency, which could contribute to the resistance profile observed (Supplementary Fig. S2D). To determine if the L528S mutation was sufficient to drive resistance, we used CRISPR/Cas9 editing to introduce the WRN L528S mutation endogenously in HCT116 cells. Two WRN L528S clones were tested and confirmed to be resistant to both AC1 and AC2 ( Fig. 2G ; Supplementary Table S1). Both AC1 and AC2 had a lower binding affinity to WRN L528S than WT WRN, and the mutation also caused a moderate decrease in the sensitivity of WRN to the compounds in the biochemical helicase assay ( Fig. 2H ; Supplementary Fig. S2E; Supplementary Tables S1 and S2). Given the proximity of these alterations to the bounds of our resolved WRN structure, we did not attempt to simulate these mutations using molecular docking. In summary, we identified three point mutations in the WRN helicase region that conferred resistance to both AC1 and AC2—one in the allosteric binding site (G729D), one at the N-terminus of the helicase region (L528S), and one in a noncoding region at the N-terminus of the helicase region (splice acceptor site resulting in WRN D526_P530del). Additionally, resistance to an endogenously introduced L528S mutation confirms that this mutation alone is sufficient to drive resistance to WRN inhibitors. WRN inhibitor HRO761 treatment leads to resistance  in vivo During our drug development program, Novartis published data on an allosteric WRN helicase inhibitor (HRO761; ref.  13 ). We confirmed HRO761’s  in vivo  efficacy in an SW48 xenograft model, observing robust TGI. However, approximately 3 weeks after treatment cessation, tumors began to regrow ( Fig. 3A ), and we hypothesized that these tumors may have acquired resistance to treatment. Consistent with this hypothesis, when we rechallenged the growing tumors with HRO761, we observed no TGI ( Fig. 3B ). We also confirmed resistance to HRO761 by dissociating a resistant tumor into a cell line and performing another xenograft experiment with HRO761 treatment (Supplementary Fig. S3A). During HRO761 treatment (and retreatment), mice remained healthy until the conclusion of the experiment (Supplementary Fig. S3B and S3C). Figure 3. We collected six tumor samples from the initial treatment group and eight tumor samples from the retreated group and performed WES to identify mutations that emerged during HRO761 treatment. We found five point mutations that were present in the WRN helicase region of both treated and retreated tumors: I852F, G729A, G729S, G729D, and F730L (Supplementary Fig. S3D). Two tumors were dissociated to generate cell lines, and mutations were identified using Sanger sequencing: L737F and I725T in one line and F730L in the other. One tumor did not have any mutations in the WRN helicase region. Most tumors had one dominating mutated allele, but some were found to have low frequencies of other mutations present (Supplementary Fig. S3D). In summary, we demonstrate that HRO761 treatment leads to rapid tumor resistance in an SW48 xenograft model, and these tumors acquire point mutations in the WRN helicase region that may confer this resistance. WRN helicase point mutations confer resistance to HRO761  in vitro To further explore mechanisms of resistance to HRO761 and generate living cellular models, we generated  in vitro  resistance to HRO761 in HCT116 and SW48 cell lines using two different methods. The first used the same resistance-generation protocol in  Fig. 2  using high doses of HRO761, which led to four mutations: G729D (HCT116 and SW48), D526_P530del (HCT116 and SW48), C727R (SW48), and F730L (SW48; Supplementary Fig. S3E). One experiment in SW48 cells resulted in a cellular population harboring both C727R and F730L mutations, whereas all other experiments yielded cell lines with a single highly dominant heterozygous mutation. The second method we employed was a ramp-up approach, in which we began HRO761 treatment at EC 50  and increased the dose by 5% to 10% until cells stopped responding to treatment. This method yielded SW48 cells with a G729D mutation and HCT116 cells with an F730L mutation, suggesting that both resistance generation approaches yield similar results (Supplementary Fig. S3F). We evaluated the resistance of WRN G729D, F730L, and C727R mutant cells to HRO761 after 72 hours of treatment and observed markedly increased viability in WRN mutants compared with parental cell lines ( Fig. 3C  and  D ; Supplementary Table S1). The biochemical helicase assay showed a significant reduction in HRO761 inhibition of the WRN mutants compared with WT WRN, providing evidence that these mutations are responsible for the observed phenotypic resistance ( Fig. 3E ; Supplementary Table S1). sources.title: Using cancer profiles to identify synthetic lethal therapeutic targets and predictive biomarkers in cancer gene dependency data.
sources.abstract: Motivation Large scale loss-of-function screens utilising CRISPR or siRNA can provide profound insights into the importance of individual genes for the survival of a cancer cell and can drive the identification of therapeutic targets and biomarkers, and the development of targeted drugs. However, the analysis of these data and the substantial bodies of metadata that relate to them, is technically challenging and typically requires substantial expertise in data science and computer coding. Results To facilitate the analysis of cancer gene dependency data by cancer biologists and clinical scientists, we have developed DepMine-a computational toolkit providing a powerful system for framing complex queries relating cancer gene dependency to the underlying genetic changes that occur in cancer cells. DepMine identifies synthetic lethal relationships between putative target genes and complex 'cancer profiles' built from user-specified combinations of mutations, copy-number variation, and expression levels, and can refine these to optimal biomarker definitions for target dependency. Availability The Python implementation of DepMine and associated data files can be obtained at https://github.com/UOSbioinformaticslab/depmine and is free to academics and Not-For-Profit organisations. The DepMine release referenced in this paper is archived as DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19570601.

1 Introduction It is estimated that between 1,000 to 4,000 genes are essential for the survival of a human cell, depending on the method used to define essentiality ( Rancati  et al.  2018 ,  Larrimore and Rancati, 2019 ,  Funk  et al.  2022 ). In cancers, as tumours develop and acquire genetic and epigenetic alterations, the tumour cell rewires its regulatory pathways and different sets of genes become essential. Examples of acquired essential genes have been identified by large-scale loss-of-function (LoF) genetic screens (e.g. DRIVE ( McDonald  et al.  2017 ) and DepMap ( Tsherniak  et al.  2017 )). The DepMap dataset, in which the mutational status and expression profiles of >19,000 genes in >1000 different cell lines has been measured, is the largest amalgamation of data for this. Although not universally true, the dependency of a tumour cell on a gene as determined by CRISPR screens, generally mirrors the susceptibility of that cell to small molecule drugs targeted against the product of that gene ( Goncalves  et al.  2020 ). Consequently, systematic analysis of the data from such screens is likely to be of great value in development of novel precision therapies and biomarkers. As cancers evolve, genetic changes are positively selected that directly impact the function of specific genes, with important consequences for the biology of the mutated tumour cell. Typically, these consist of loss-of-function (LoF) mutations in tumour suppressors or gain-of-function (GoF) mutations in proto-oncogenes. LoF of tumour suppressors can be targeted by synthetic sickness/lethality (SSL), a negative genetic interaction whereby a cell can survive the loss of protein product from the tumour suppressor or from its synthetic lethal partner gene, but not from both ( Lord and Ashworth, 2017 ,  O’Neil  et al.  2017 ). The best-known example is treatment of BRCA1/2 deficient tumours in breast, ovarian and other tumours with PARP inhibitors ( Mateo  et al.  2019 ). Generally, SSL relates pairs of genes, with one gene being the therapeutic target in cells where the other gene is defective. However, SSL may also relate a target gene to a phenotype or complex genetic state as in the identification of Werner syndrome ATP-dependent helicase (WRN) as a synthetic lethal (SSL) target in tumours displaying microsatellite instability (MSI) ( Chan  et al.  2019 ,  Picco  et al.  2021 ); a Werner inhibitor ( NCT05838768 ) is now in Phase 1 clinical development for MSI solid tumours ( Ferretti  et al.  2024 ). Oncogene addiction occurs when a tumour cell becomes dependent on the presence of an activated proto-oncogene with a gain-of-function (GoF) mutation ( Weinstein and Joe 2008 ). Oncogenes can often be targeted directly, but the therapeutic response to even highly specific and potent drugs is often very mixed across patient populations. Synthetic dosage lethality (SDL), where activation of a gene (e.g. the oncogene) is synthetically lethal with LoF of another gene, can be utilised to identify biomarkers where oncogene-directed therapy is most likely to be effective ( Megchelenbrink  et al.  2015 ). Given the cost and technical challenge posed by mounting ‘wet’ screens to find SSL relationships, there has been substantial interest in developing analysis pipelines that exploit large cancer cell-line or patient genetic and clinical data collections such as TCGA ( Liu  et al.  2018 ) and COSMIC ( Tate  et al.  2019 )) to identify synthetic lethality relationships, and/or targetable oncogenes and response-predictive biomarkers computationally–for example ( Ryan  et al.  2014 ,  Shao  et al.  2016 ,  Benstead-Hume  et al.  2019 ,  Das  et al.  2019 ,  Lee  et al.  2021 ,  Srivatsa  et al.  2022 ,  Wang  et al.  2022 ,  Markowska  et al.  2023 ,  Pacini  et al.  2024 ,  Wooller  et al.  2024 ). To date these methods generally focus on identifying synthetically lethal gene pairs. Here we describe  DepMine , a computational toolkit for the analysis of cancer gene dependency data to identify synthetically lethal relationships and the genetic backgrounds in which they might best be exploited.  DepMine  goes substantially beyond pair-wise SSL relationships by allowing specification of complex ‘cancer profiles’ which can be used to probe cancer gene dependency data for synthetic lethality with a target gene of interest within cell lines that match the profile. As well as individual gene descriptors, (i.e. GoF or LoF mutations), individual gene or regional copy number variation (CNV), gene expression levels, and cellular properties (e.g. tissue type, mutational signatures, age, sex), can all be combined in the profile definition using a simple set-theory based algebraic formalism. Profiles can be automatically refined to optimise the strength and breadth of the predicted SSL effect with a target gene, thereby defining the genetic backgrounds in which inhibitors or degraders are most likely to be effective.  DepMine  profiles can then be used as biomarkers to select cancer cell lines or patient samples, in which precision therapies of known drug targets, or specific inhibitors of novel drug targets, are most likely to be of therapeutic benefit. 2 Methods 2.1 Data sources 
 DepMine  utilises publicly available datasets centred on DepMap 2023Q2 that can be independently downloaded by the user. The source data files are given in the  Supplementary Data , available as  supplementary material  at  Bioinformatics  online. Expression thresholds are calculated with an ancillary program  expr_scorer.py , and mutational signatures for the cell lines documented in DepMap are calculated using  SigProfilerAssignment    https://osf.io/mz79v/wiki/home/  ( Díaz-Gay  et al.  2023 ) with context_type = 96 and genome_build=GRCh38. The input .vcf files required by  SigProfilerAssignment  are generated from the DepMap mutation data by an ancillary program,  MakeVCF.py . 2.2 Cancer profiles At the heart of  DepMine  is a set-theory based system in which membership of a set by a cell line is determined by whether or not that cell line matches a user-defined ‘cancer profile’.  DepMine  cancer profiles are logical statements constructed from primitive functions that determine the truth or otherwise of postulates about the tissue origin of the cell line, sex and/or age of the patient from which it was derived, and the genetic status or expression level of one or more genes within that cell line. A function returning the Universal Set–i.e. all the available cell lines—is also provided. Primitive functions can be combined by the set operations: union  | , intersection  &  and exclusion  ^ , and expressions can be fully bracketed to achieve cancer profiles of considerable complexity (see  RESULTS ). The definitions of all DepMine cancer profiles referenced in this paper are provided in  Table 1  in the  Supplementary Data , available as  supplementary material  at  Bioinformatics  online, and will provide the reader with sufficient examples to define their own.
