sources.title: SMARCA4/2 loss reduces BCL-xL expression and confers a druggable MCL1 dependency in cancer.
sources.abstract: SMARCA4 (BRG1) and SMARCA2 (BRM) are the mutually exclusive ATPase subunits of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complexes, often altered in cancers. Concurrent loss of SMARCA4/2 is found in some aggressive cancer types, including small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT), a rare and lethal ovarian cancer affecting young women, and a subset of non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLCs), associated with chemotherapy resistance and poor outcome. Through a functional genetic approach, we identified that inhibition of MCL1, an anti-apoptotic protein of the BCL-2 family, is synthetic lethal with SMARCA4/2 loss in these cancer cells. MCL1 suppression by RNAi or a small molecule inhibitor, S63845, selectively induced apoptosis in SMARCA4/2-deficient SCCOHT and NSCLC cells but not in SMARCA4/2-proficient controls. Mechanistically, SMARCA4/2 directly promotes mRNA expression of BCL-xL, encoding another key anti-apoptotic protein of the BCL-2 family; SMARCA4/2 loss therefore results in downregulation of BCL-xL, leading to MCL1 dependency to suppress apoptosis in these cancer cells. Furthermore, single-agent treatment of S63845 resulted in significant suppression of tumor growth in patient-derived xenografts of SMARCA4/2-deficient NSCLC and SCCOHT. Collectively, our work uncovered MCL1 as a synthetic lethal target in SMARCA4/2-deficient cancers that may be exploited therapeutically.
sources.full_text_excerpt:
Introduction The switch/sucrose non-fermentable (SWI/SNF) complexes utilize chemical energy through ATP hydrolysis to remodel nucleosome positioning and conformation to control gene expression 1 – 3 . The abnormalities in different SWI/SNF subunits are implicated in the development of a broad range of human malignancies 4 , 5 . SMARCA4 and SMARCA2 are the two mutually exclusive SWI/SNF ATPases that are frequently altered in cancers. Inactivating  SMARCA4  mutations are found in ~7.2% of human cancers, including ~100% of small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT), a rare and aggressive ovarian cancer subtype, and ~10% of non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLCs) 6 – 9 . In contrast,  SMARCA2  is often lost through epigenetic silencing, which is thought to cooperate with SMARCA4 deficiency for tumorigenesis in SCCOHT as well as in a subset of NSCLCs and other poorly differentiated aggressive cancers 10 – 15 . SMARCA4/2-deficient cancers often lack known druggable mutations and exhibit resistance to standard chemotherapy regimens, making them difficult to treat 6 , 16 , 17 . In search of alternative treatment strategies, previous studies have shown that SMARCA4/2-deficient cancers rely on epigenetic reprogramming and are responsive to inhibitors targeting the polycomb repressive complex 2, histone deacetylases, bromodomain-containing protein 4, and histone demethylase KDM6 in preclinical models 18 – 22 . We and others also found that these cancer cells are sensitive to drugs targeting receptor tyrosine kinases 23 , CDK4/6 24 , 25 , arginine metabolism 26 , as well as oxidative phosphorylation and glutamine metabolism 27 . However, most of these inhibitors primarily suppress proliferation, and drug resistance is expected to arise quickly - underscoring the need for novel therapeutic strategies that actively induce cancer cell death to achieve tumor eradication. Anti-apoptotic proteins of the B-cell lymphoma-2 (BCL-2) family are promising therapeutic targets in cancer, as dysregulation of apoptosis – resulting from an imbalance between pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic factors - is a central hallmark of tumor development and progression 28 – 30 . Two key BCL-2 family proteins, myeloid cell leukemia sequence 1 (MCL1) and BCL2 Like 1 (BCL2L1, commonly referred to as BCL-x), coordinate in regulating BAK/BAX-dependent apoptosis and promoting cell survival 31 – 33 . MCL1 is anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane through its hydrophobic tail 34  and sequesters the proapoptotic proteins BAK/BAX via its hydrophobic groove in BCL-2 homology (BH) 3 domain 35 . BCL-x, encoded by the  BCL2L1  gene, has two isoforms produced through alternative splicing: BCL-xL and BCL-xS. The long isoform BCL-xL contains BH1-BH3 domains and exerts its anti-apoptotic function by inhibiting activation of BAX, like MCL1 36 , 37 . In contrast, the short isoform BCL-xS is a pro-apoptotic protein – it lacks the BH1 and BH2 domains and binds to BCL-xL, causing the release of the pro-apoptotic BAK 38 . BCL-xL is the most abundant BCL-x protein in most cells. Overexpression of MCL1 and BCL-xL is widely observed in various cancers associated with poor prognosis and therapy resistance 39 – 41 . Therefore, a range of therapeutic agents targeting these anti-apoptotic proteins—such as small-molecule inhibitors (e.g.,  S63845  and Navitoclax)—have been developed to overcome resistance and improve clinical outcomes 42 , 43 . In this study, we uncovered that SMARCA4/2-deficient ovarian and lung cancer cells are selectively dependent on MCL1 through a systematic approach. We validated the selective MCL1 dependency in these cancer cells and tumors and uncovered the underlying mechanism, supporting MCL1 as a potential druggable target in SMARCA4/2-deficient cancers. Results SMARCA4/2-deficient lung and ovarian cancer cells are selectively sensitive to MCL1 inhibition To systematically uncover genetic vulnerabilities in SMARCA4/2-deficient cancer cells, we analyzed publicly available RNA-sequencing data from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) 44 , 45  to stratify 111 ovarian and lung cancer cell lines into two groups based on  SMARCA4  mutation status and  SMARCA2  expression levels (see Methods). The lung cancer panel included 9 SMARCA4/2-deficient NSCLC cell lines 46  and 65 SMARCA4/2-proficient lines. The ovarian cancer cell line panel comprised 5 SMARCA4/2-deficient lines—including three SCCOHT cell lines (BIN-67, SCCOHT-1, and COV434) 14 , 47  and two dedifferentiated ovarian cancer lines (TOV-112D and OVK18) 20 , 47 —alongside 32 SMARCA4/2-proficient lines. Next, we analyzed the genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screens in these cell lines from the Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap,  https://depmap.org ) and used the ΔCERES (difference in the CERES scores), a metric that quantifies the difference in gene dependency between two cell line groups, to measure this selective lethality. We found that  MCL1 , but not other BCL-2 family members, was one of the top-ranked candidate genes whose knockout was selective lethal to SMARCA4/2-deficient cells in both cancer types (ΔCERES < −0.25, -log 10 (p-value)>2) (Fig.  1a  and Supplementary Fig.  1 ), suggesting a unique role of MCL1 in promoting the survival of cancer cells with SMARCA4/2 loss. Furthermore, we queried the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) database 48  for the available cell line drug response data corresponding to the lung and ovarian cancer cell lines used in the CCLE dataset in Fig.  1a . Consistently, SMARCA4/2-deficient cells exhibited significantly lower half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC50) for three different MCL1 inhibitors (AZD5991, MIM1, and UMI-77) compared to SMARCA4/2-proficient cells (Fig.  1b ). Together, these findings suggest that SMARCA4/2-deficient cancer cells are particularly vulnerable to MCL1 inhibition. Fig. 1 SMARCA4/2-deficient lung and ovarian cancer cells are selectively sensitive to MCL1 inhibition. a  Volcano plot of DepMap genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screens showing differential gene dependency (ΔCERES) between SMARCA4/2-deficient and -proficient NSCLC and ovarian cancer cell lines (A4/2ᴰᵉᶠ vs A4/2ᴾʳᵒ). All BCL2 family proteins were labeled.  b  Violin plots showing IC₅₀ values (log₂) of MCL1 inhibitors in SMARCA4/2-dual deficient (A4/2ᴰᵉᶠ) and -proficient (A4/2ᴾʳᵒ) lung and ovarian cancer cell lines (the plotted cell lines represent the common set found in both the GDSC and CCLE databases). For AZD5991,  n  = 44 (A4/2ᴾʳᵒ) vs 7 (A4/2ᴰᵉᶠ); for MIM1,  n  = 48 (A4/2ᴾʳᵒ) vs 10 (A4/2ᴰᵉᶠ); for UMI-77,  n  = 45 (A4/2ᴾʳᵒ) vs 7 (A4/2ᴰᵉᶠ). Each point represents a cell line (gray: lung; red: ovary). ** p  < 0.01; *** p  < 0.001, unpaired two-tailed Student’s  t -test. Colony formation ( c ) and immunoblot ( d ) analyses of NSCLC cells expressing control or MCL1 shRNAs. MCL1 knockdown suppressed long-term growth and increased cleaved PARP in SMARCA4/2-deficient H1703 cells but not in proficient H1437 cells. Colony formation ( e ) and immunoblot ( f ) analyses of ovarian cancer cells expressing control or MCL1 shRNAs. SMARCA4/2-deficient SCCOHT-1 and BIN-67 cells were sensitive to MCL1 knockdown, whereas SMARCA4/2-proficient OVCAR4 high-grade serous carcinoma cells were less affected. Colony formation ( g ) and cell viability ( h ) assays showing that SMARCA4/2-deficient NSCLC lines (A427, H661, H1703, H23) were more sensitive to the selective MCL1 inhibitor  S63845  than proficient lines (H358, H1437, HCC827).  i  Tumor growth curves of SMARCA4/2-deficient NSCLC PDX (TM01563) models treated with vehicle or  S63845  (25 mg/kg, intraperitoneally, twice weekly).  S63845  significantly suppressed tumor growth,  n  = 3 (Vehicle) vs 4 ( S63845 ). Error bars, mean ± s.d.; **** p  < 0.0001, two-way ANOVA. Colony formation ( j ) and cell viability ( k ) assays showing that SMARCA4/2-deficient SCCOHT cells (COV434, SCCOHT-1, BIN-67) were markedly sensitive to  S63845  compared with OVCAR4 and FT190 controls.  l  Tumor growth curves of SMARCA4/2-deficient SCCOHT PDX (NRTO-1) models treated with vehicle or  S63845   n  = 5 (Vehicle) vs 5 ( S63845 ), showing significant tumor growth inhibition in vivo. Error bars, mean ± s.d.; **** p  < 0.0001, two-way ANOVA. Validating this, knockdown of MCL1 using two independent shRNAs strongly suppressed growth in long-term colony formation assay in SMARCA4/2-deficient NSCLC cells (H1703) but had little effect on SMARCA4/2-proficient NSCLC cells (H1437) (Fig.  1c  and Supplementary Data  1 ). As expected, MCL1 knockdown increased apoptosis as indicated by elevated levels of cleaved PARP (Fig.  1d ). A similar trend was seen in ovarian cancer: SMARCA4/2-deficient SCCOHT cell lines, SCCOHT-1 and BIN-67, were much more sensitive to MCL1 knockdown compared to SMARCA4/2-proficient OVCAR4 high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) cells (Fig.  1e–f ). In line with the above RNAi results, the selective MCL1 inhibitor  S63845 42 , 49  elicited pronounced sensitivity in SMARCA4/2-deficient NSCLC lines (A427, H661, H1703, H23) compared to their proficient counterparts (H358, H1437, HCC827) in colony-formation and viability assays (Fig.  1g, h  and Supplementary Data  1 ). Furthermore,  S63845  treatment induced a partial but significant inhibition of tumor growth in a SMARCA4/2-deficient NSCLC patient-derived xenograft (PDX) model 27  (Fig.  1i  and Supplementary Data  1 ). Similar results were also obtained in ovarian cancer models, where SMARCA4/2-deficient SCCOHT cells (COV434, SCCOHT-1, BIN-67) displayed marked sensitivity to  S63845 , contrasting with the reduced sensitivity of SMARCA4/2-proficient controls, including OVCAR4 and FT190, an immortalized but non-transformed fallopian cell line (Fig.  1j, k ). Single agent treatment of  S63845  also significantly suppressed the growth of SCCOHT xenografts in vivo (Fig.  1l ). Together, these above data validated that SMARCA4/2-deficient cancers are vulnerable to MCL1 inhibition both in vitro and in vivo. SMARCA4/2 loss causes the selective sensitivity to MCL1 inhibition Our above results established the correlation of SMARCA4/2 deficiency and sensitivity to MCL1 inhibition. We next investigated whether SMARCA4/2 loss contributes to this selective dependency on MCL1 inhibition. Supporting this, re-expression of SMARCA4 in SMARCA4/2-deficient A427 and H1703 NSCLC cells conferred resistance to  S63845  in both cell viability and colony formation assays (Fig.  2a–d  and Supplementary Data  1 ), which was accompanied with suppressed apoptosis as indicated by reduced expression of cleaved PARP upon  S63845  treatment (Fig.  2e, f ). In contrast to lung cancer cells, restoration of SMARCA4 in SCCOHT cells is known to cause strong growth repression 14 , 24 , making long-term growth assays challenging. Nevertheless, short-term  S63845  treatment assay also showed that ectopic SMARCA4 expression partially alleviated apoptosis induced by MCL1 inhibition (Fig.  2g ). Conversely, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated  SMARCA4  knockout in SMARCA4/2-proficient FT190 and H1437 cells partially sensitized them to  S63845  although not statistically significant, and  SMARCA2  knockdown using two independent shRNAs in these  SMARCA4  knockout cells further increased their drug sensitivities (Supplementary Fig.  2  and Supplementary Data  1 ). Notably,  SMARCA4  knockout in these cells resulted in reduced SMARCA2 expression, which requires further investigations but nevertheless supports the causal role of these two paralogs in regulating  S63845  sensitivity. Taken together, these data indicate that SMARCA4/2 loss in lung and ovarian cancer cells results in selective sensitivity to MCL1 inhibition, at least partly mediated through enhanced apoptosis. Fig. 2 SMARCA4 re-expression reduces sensitivity to MCL1 inhibition in SMARCA4/2-deficient cells. Cell viability ( a ,  b ),  n  = 3–6, Error bars, mean ± s.d., colony formation ( c ) and immunoblot ( d ) showing that re-expression of SMARCA4 in SMARCA4/2-deficient NSCLC cells (A427, H1703) conferred resistance to  S63845  compared with vector controls. Immunoblot analyses verifying  SMARCA4 restoration in  A427, H1703. Immunoblots of A427 ( e ), H1703 ( f ), and SCCOHT-1 ( g ) cells with or without SMARCA4 treated with or without  S63845  for 24 hours. SMARCA4/2 loss results in BCL-xL deficiency Next, we investigated the mechanism underlying this selective MCL1 dependency of SMARCA4/2 loss. Given the well-established role of MCL1 in apoptosis control and SMARCA4/2 in gene expression regulation, we hypothesized that SMARCA4/2 loss may result in either aberrant MCL1 expression or dysregulation of other BCL-2 members, leading to MCL1 dependency. To investigate this, we analyzed RNA-seq datasets from SMARCA4/2-proficient NSCLC H358 cells to profile BCL-2 family gene expression before and after  SMARCA4  knockdown 50 . In parallel, we also examined how restoring SMARCA4 or SMARCA2 affected the expression of these genes in SMARCA4/2-deficient models, including NSCLC (A427, H1703) and SCCOHT (COV434, SCCOHT-1, BIN-67) cell lines 24 , 51 . As shown in Fig.  3a , among the 12 key BCL-2 family members,  BCL2L1  was the only gene obviously regulated by SMARCA4 or SMARCA2 across all cell lines – downregulated upon SMARCA4 knockdown and upregulated upon restoration of SMARCA4 or SMARCA2, whereas MCL1 expression remained largely unaffected. Fig. 3 SMARCA4/2 deficiency mediates synthetic lethality with MCL1 inhibition through downregulation of  BCL-xL  expression. a  Expression levels of apoptosis-associated genes in ovarian and lung cancer cell lines ± SMARCA4/2 restoration or SMARCA4 knockout. Each dot represents a gene. For all cell lines presented, each condition includes ≥3 technical replicates. Ctrl: control, A2: SMARCA2, A4: SMARCA4.  b 
 BCL2L1  mRNA levels in SCCOHT ( n  = 13) and HGSC ( n  = 21) patient tumor samples. *** p  < 0.001, unpaired two-tailed Student’s  t -test.  c  Real-time PCR analysis of  BCL-xL  mRNA levels in SMARCA4/2-deficient cell lines expressing vector control (Ctrl), SMARCA4 (A4) or SMARCA2 (A2).  n  = 3, error bars: mean ± s.d., * p  < 0.05; ** p  < 0.01; **** p  < 0.0001, Brown-Forsythe and Welch ANOVA.  d  Immunoblots of indicated cell lines ± SMARCA4 re-expression measuring MCL1 and BCL-xL protein levels. Actin was used as a loading control.  e  Western blots of 21 NSCLC cell lines using antibodies against SMARCA4, SMARCA2, MCL1, and BCL-xL. HSP90 served as a loading control. A4, SMARCA4; A4/2, SMARCA4/2; Pro, proficient; Def, deficient.  f  Representative genome browser tracks showing SMARCA4/2, H3K27Ac ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq peaks at the  BCL2L1  locus in BIN-67 and H1703 cells re-expressing SMARCA4/2. BCL2L1  encodes BCL-xL and BCL-xS isoforms that arise from alternative splicing and have opposing functions in inhibiting and promoting apoptosis, respectively 52 . Closer examination of the RNA-seq data showed that the dominant isoform in BIN-67 cells is  BCL-xL , which was upregulated upon SMARCA4 restoration and was ~ 40-fold more abundant than  BCL-xS  (Supplementary Fig.  3a, b ). Given that  BCL2 , another key anti-apoptotic protein, was also expressed at low levels among all cell lines independent of SMARCA4/2 status (Fig.  3a ), these observations highlight the potential key role of  BCL2L1  regulation by SMARCA4/2 in this context of MCL1 dependency. In line with these cell lines' data, analysis of the RNA-seq datasets of SCCOHT 17  and TCGA HGSC tumors 53  showed that SCCOHT tumors expressed significantly lower  BCL2L1  than HGSCs (Fig.  3b ). These observations suggest that SMARCA4/2 loss causes reduced BCL-xL expression, leading to increased dependency on MCL1 in these cancer cells to suppress apoptosis. Further supporting the regulation of BCL-xL by SMARCA4/2, ectopic expression of SMARCA4 in SMARCA4/2-deficient SCCOHT and NSCLC cell lines significantly increased  BCL-xL  mRNA levels, as shown by qPCR (Fig.  3c  and Supplementary Fig.  3c ), and concurrently a trend of BCL-xL protein level elevation (Fig.  3d ). Moreover, analysis of a panel of 21 NSCLC cell lines revealed a positive correlation between SMARCA4/2 expression status and BCL-xL protein levels (Fig.  3e  and Supplementary Fig.  4 ) - while SMARCA4/2-deficient cells exhibited the lowest BCL-xL expression, among SMARCA4-deficient lines that retain SMARCA2 expression, BCL-xL expression positively correlated with SMARCA2 levels, which is in line with the functional redundancy between SMARCA4 and SMARCA2 in regulating  BCL-xL  expression (Fig.  3c ). Together, these results indicate that SMARCA4/2 loss results in reduced  BCL2L1  expression leading to BCL-xL reduction, which may underlie MCL1 dependency. SMARCA4/2 directly controls chromatin accessibility of the BCL2L1 locus Given the chromatin remodeling role of SWI/SNF, we also examined the chromatin architecture of the  BCL2L1  locus and its potential direct regulation by SMARCA4/2. Indeed, upon SMARCA4 restoration, ChIP-seq analysis in BIN-67 cells 51  revealed SMARCA4 occupancy at the promoter and regulatory regions of  BCL2L1  (Fig.  3f ), suggesting that SMARCA4 directly regulates  BCL2L1  expression. Supporting this, we found that ChIP-seq signals of H3K27Ac, a chromatin mark associated with active promoters and enhancers, were elevated at these regions upon re-expression of SMARCA4 or SMARCA2 in both BIN-67 and H1703 cells 25 . In addition, the Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) peaks at these genomic regions were also elevated upon restoration of SMARCA4 or SMARCA2 in BIN-67 and H1703 cells (Fig.  3f ), indicating enhanced chromatin accessibility at the  BCL2L1  locus when SMARCA4/2 was present. These data support a model in which SMARCA4/2 promotes  BCL2L1  transcription by directly remodeling chromatin structure at its gene locus. BCL-xL deficiency underlies the synthetic lethal interaction between MCL1 inhibition and SMARCA4/2 loss Our data thus far suggest that SMARCA4/2 loss leads to reduced BCL-xL expression, which could limit the total anti-apoptotic capacity in SMARCA4/2-deficient cancer cells and render their sensitivity to MCL1 inhibition. If this hypothesis is correct, forced elevation of BCL-xL should rescue these cancer cells from MCL1 inhibition. Indeed, ectopic expression of BCL-xL conferred resistance to  S63845  treatment in H1703 and SCCOHT-1 cells in both colony-formation and cell viability assays (Fig.  4a–d  and Supplementary Data  1 ) and suppressed apoptosis induction (Fig.  4e, f ). MCL1 overexpression also yielded a similar phenotype, although the effect was less pronounced at higher concentrations of  S63845 . This is expected, as  S63845  targets MCL1, and higher concentrations of the drug may saturate the available MCL1 pool. Similarly, ectopic expression of BCL-xL protected H1703 cells from the growth inhibition and apoptosis induction caused by a shRNA targeting the 3′UTR of  MCL1  (Fig.  4g, h  and Supplementary Data  1 ). As a control, ectopic expression of an  MCL1  cDNA lacking 3′UTR also rescued these phenotypes induced by this shRNA against  MCL1  (Fig.  4g, h  and Supplementary Data  1 ). Fig. 4 BCL-xL deficiency predominantly contributes to MCL1 dependency. Colony formation assays of H1703 ( a ) and SCCOHT-1 ( b ) cells stably expressing pLX304- GFP , pLX304- MCL1 , or pLX304- BCL-xL , cultured with indicated concentrations of MCL1 inhibitor for 14 days. Cell viability assays of H1703 ( c ) and SCCOHT-1 ( d ) cells stably expressing pLX304- GFP , pLX304- MCL1 , or pLX304- BCL-xL , treated with MCL1 inhibitor for 5 days.  n  = 3, error bars: mean ± s.d. Western blot analysis of H1703 ( e ) and SCCOHT-1 ( f ) cells expressing the indicated constructs and treated with increasing doses of MCL1 inhibitor for 24 hours. Blots were probed for SMARCA4, cleaved PARP, MCL1, BCL-xL, cleaved caspase-3, and HSP90. The ectopically expressed proteins were highlighted by the arrows. Colony formation assay ( g ) and immunoblot analysis ( h ) of H1703 cells expressing the indicated constructs and co-infected with  pLKO  control or  MCL1  3′UTR-targeting shRNA. Western blots probed with antibodies against SMARCA4, cleaved PARP, MCL1, BCL-xL, and HSP90.  i  Colony formation assays of A427 and H1703 cells ± SMARCA4 re-expression, cultured with MCL1 inhibitor ± 1 μM WEHI-539 (BCL-xL selective inhibitor) for 14 days. All plates were fixed at the same time. While our above data established that reduced BCL-xL expression in SMARCA4/2-deficient cancer cells contributes to their increased dependency on MCL1 for apoptosis inhibition, it remained unclear if this is the main cause since SMARCA4/2 regulate expression of diverse genes and pathways. To test this, we took advantage of the fact that SMARCA4/2-deficient NSCLC cells can better tolerate restoration of SMARCA4 and performed “double rescue” experiments. As shown in Fig.  4i , while restoration of SMARCA4 in both A427 and H1703 cells conferred resistance to MCL1 inhibition by  S63845 , addition of WEHI-539, a selective BCL-xL inhibitor, completely reversed their sensitivity to  S63845 . Importantly, WEHI-539 treatment alone did not suppress the growth of the cells. These results indicate that reduced BCL-xL expression in SMARCA4/2-deficient cancer cells is the main underlying cause for their dependency on MCL1 (Supplementary Fig.  5 ). Discussion In this study, we identified and validated MCL1 as a druggable dependency in SMARCA4/2-deficient ovarian and lung cancers. We demonstrated that this selective MCL1 dependency is associated with the downregulation of BCL-xL induced by SMARCA4/2 loss and may be exploited therapeutically using MCL1 inhibitors. MCL1/BCL-xL ratio has been previously shown to predict the efficiency of MCL1 inhibition in NSCLC cell lines, although the genetic events causing this MCL1/BCL-xL imbalance were not known 54 . Our findings are in line with this study and provide the mechanistic link between SMARCA4/2 deficiency and altered MCL1/BCL-xL ratio. We demonstrated that SMARCA4/2 directly regulates  BCL-xL  mRNA expression, and SMARCA4/2 loss thus results in BCL-xL deficiency leading to MCL1 dependency in both SCCOHT and NSCLC cells. While SMARCA4 has been shown to influence splicing programs, no differential BCL2L1 (BCL-x) splicing upon SMARCA4 perturbation was detected 55 . Consistent with this, SMARCA4 restoration in SCCOHT cells increased mRNA expression of both isoforms, with BCL-xL being the dominant isoform expressed in these cancer cells. Forced re-expression of SMARCA4 conferred resistance to MCL1 inhibition in SMARCA4/2-deficient cancer cells. This resistance was reversed by co-treatment with a selective BCL-xL inhibitor. supporting the causal role of reduced BCL-xL expression in mediating the synthetic lethal interaction between SMARCA4/2 loss and MCL1 inhibition. The MCL1 inhibitor  S63845  has demonstrated significant anti-tumor activity in models of multiple myeloma, lymphoma, and myeloid leukemia, where 45-68% of cell lines tested exhibited high sensitivity to  S63845  (IC 50  < 0.1 μM) 42 , 56 . Its derivative,  S64315 , is currently being evaluated in clinical trials for these hematologic malignancies 56 . While our results showed that  S63845  was also highly effective in targeting SMARCA4/2-deficient SCCOHT and NSCLC cells in vitro (IC 50  < 0.1 μM), it had modest anti-tumor activity in vivo against the PDX models. Future studies with SMARCA4/2-proficient models as controls may help better establish this potential utility of  S63845  for SMARCA4/2-deficient tumors. This modest in vivo anti-tumor activity of  S63845  could be potentially attributed to limited drug penetration due to the compactness of the solid tumor, in contrast to leukemic cancers. Treatment strategies combining MCL1 inhibitors and other agents may help overcome this and enhance its clinical utility. In fact,  S63845  is mostly used in combination with other drugs, such as nucleoside azacitidine 57  and BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax 58 . Notably, our previous study demonstrated that the loss of SMARCA4/2 confers resistence to chemotherapy-induced apoptosis in lung and ovarian cancers due to downregulation of ITPR3, a critical ion channel that mediates Ca²⁺ flux from the endoplasmic reticulum to mitochondria—a process essential for apoptosis induction 17 . Therefore, combining cisplatin with an MCL1 inhibitor may enhance tumor cell sensitivity by promoting apoptosis in these SMARCA4/2-deficient cancers with BCL-xL deficiency. Notably, a previous study reported that separase-dependent cleavage of MCL1 and BCL-xL can induce apoptosis and cell death in shortened mitosis, indicating that these factors also participate in cell cycle regulation 59 . Thus, combined MCL1 and CDK4/6 inhibitors may have a synergistic effect targeting SMARCA4/2-deficient cancers. Given that CDK4/6 have been shown to be effective in suppressing preclinical models of these SWI/SNF-deficient cancers 24 , 25 , 60 , such potential combination strategies warrant future investigations. In summary, our study uncovered MCL1 as a synthetic lethal target in SMARCA4/2-deficient lung and ovarian cancers. Given the clinical advancement of MCL1 inhibitors in hematologic malignancies, MCL1 inhibition may also be considered for the treatment of SMARCA4/2-deficient cancers. Methods Cell culture Cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11995-065) or Roswell Park Memorial Institute 1640 Medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cat# 11875-093) supplemented with 7% fetal bovine serum (Sigma, Cat# F1051), 2 mM L-glutamine (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 25030-081), and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 15140-122) at 37 °C and 5% CO₂. Mycoplasma contamination was routinely tested using MycoAlert (Lonza, LT07-318). Short tandem repeat (STR) profiling confirmed cell line identity. Compounds and antibodies S63845  (HY-100741) and WEHI-539 (HY-15607) were from MedChemExpress. Antibodies against β-Actin (sc-47778), HSP90 (sc-13119), SMARCA2 (11996), MCL1 (94296S), BCL-xL (2764), cleaved PARP (5625), and cleaved caspase-3 (9664) were used at 1:1000; SMARCA4 (A300-813A) was used at 1:5000. Plasmids and lentiviral transduction shRNAs and ORFs were from the Mission TRC library (Sigma) via McGill Genetic Perturbation Service (GPS) and McGill Platform for Cellular Perturbation (MPCP). Constructs included shMCL1#1 (TRCN0000196390), shMCL1#2 (TRCN0000197024), pLKO_TRC001, pReceiver-Lv105, pReceiver-SMARCA4 (GeneCopoeia), and pLX304 vectors ( MCL1  ccsbBroad304_00985,  BCL-xL  CCSBBroad304_053D1_C02,  GFP  ccsbBroad304_07515; Transomic). Lentivirus was produced in 293 T cells via CaCl₂-mediated transfection with psPAX2 and pMD2.G. Supernatants were harvested 24 and 36 h post-transfection and used to infect target cells. Selection was done with puromycin (2 μg/mL) or blasticidin (20 μg/mL) for 2–4 days. RNA isolation and qRT-PCR Trizol (Invitrogen) was used to isolate total RNA and the Maxima First Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Thermo Scientific) was used to convert mRNA to cDNA. qRT-PCR (Quantitative real-time reverse transcription PCR) was performed using SYBR® Green master mix (Roche) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Relative mRNA levels of the indicated genes were determined by normalizing to the housekeeping gene  ACTB . The sequences of the qRT-PCR primers are as follows: ACTB_Forward (Fwd), GTTGTCGACGACGAGCG; ACTB_Reverse (Rev), GCACAGAGCCTCGCCTT; BCL-xL_Forward (Fwd), CCTAAGGCGGATTTGAATAATCTT; BCL-xL_Reverse (Rev), CCCGGTTGCTCTGAGACATT. Colony formation assay Cells (2–8 × 10⁴/well) were seeded in 6-well plates. Drugs or vehicle were added the next day and refreshed every 3 days for 10–14 days. Colonies were fixed in 3.75% formaldehyde and stained with 0.1% crystal violet. All colony formation assays were independently reproduced at least two to three times and quantified by the ImageJ plugin ColonyArea ( https://github.com/Turku-BioImaging/ColonyArea ) as shown in Supplementary Data  1 . Cell viability assay Cells (1000–6000/well) were plated in 96-well plates and treated after 24 hours with compound dilutions. After 4 days, viability was measured by CellTiter-Blue (Promega) at 560/590 nm in a Tecan Infinite M200 PRO multimode microplate reader. Data were normalized to vehicle controls. Immunoblotting Cells were lysed in SDS buffer 24 h post-treatment. Lysates were separated using NuPAGE gels (Thermo Fisher) and transferred to membranes. β-Actin and HSP90 served as loading controls. Uncropped scans of Western blots are shown in Supplementary Fig.  6 . Transcriptome and chromatin profiling RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, and ChIP-seq data were obtained from  GSE151026 ,  GSE117735 ,  GSE121755 , and  GSE162611 . Reads were aligned to hg19 using STAR (v2.6.1c) 61  and quantified using featureCounts (v1.6.4) 62 . IGV 63  was used for visualization. RNA-seq read counts from 13 SCCOHT tumors 17 , 64  and 379 ovarian cancer tumors retrieved from UCSC Xena ( http://xena.ucsc.edu/ ) were processed uniformly using the same computational pipeline. The fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads (FPKM) values were calculated as (RCg × 10⁹)/(RCpc × L), in which RCg is the number of reads mapped to the gene; RCpc is the number of reads mapped to protein-coding genes; and L is the mean of the lengths of the gene isoforms. ggplot2 (v3.3.3) 65  was used for visualization. Cell lines were defined as  SMARCA4/2 -dual deficient according to literature references (SCCOHT-1, COV434, BIN-67, TOV112D, OVK18, H1703, A427, H522, H23) 46  or if the cell lines displayed damaging mutations on  SMARCA4  and low  SMARCA2  expression (Log 2 (TPM + 1) < 3). Isoform-level quantification of  BCL-xL  and  BCL-xS  from the RNA-seq dataset in BIN-67 cells ( GSE151026 ) was conducted: reads were aligned to hg19 with STAR, and transcript abundances were normalized to total counts per sample to generate counts per million (CPM). A Sashimi plot was generated to visualize the alternative splicing (AS) pattern of the  BCL2L1  gene. In vivo experiments PDX tumors (NRTO-1, TM01563) were implanted in NSG mice. Mice ( n  = 3–5/group) received vehicle or 25 mg/kg  S63845  (intraperitoneal injection) twice weekly.  S63845  was dissolved in 25 mM HCl and 20% hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin. Tumor size was measured twice weekly by blinded assessors. Procedures were approved by the McGill Animal Care Committee. Statistical analysis Statistical significance was tested using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s  t -test when comparing two groups, and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Dunnett’s post hoc test for multiple groups.  p -values: * p  < 0.05, ** p  < 0.01, *** p  < 0.001, **** p  < 0.0001. sources.title: Synthetic lethality in cancer: mechanism exploration and therapeutic applications.
sources.abstract: Synthetic lethality (SL) is a genetic interaction phenomenon in which a cell can survive when either of two genes is individually mutated, but simultaneous disruption of both genes leads to cell death. This phenomenon reveals the redundancy and complementarity among gene functions and provides a theoretical basis for precision cancer therapies targeting specific genetic defects. The SL approach achieves the selective elimination of cancer cells by targeting the synergistic survival pathways on which tumor-specific genetic defects rely. This review highlights the core molecular mechanisms of SL in DNA damage repair, cell cycle checkpoint regulation, metabolic reprogramming, and epigenetic regulation; summarizes target discovery strategies based on high-throughput functional genomics and computational biology; and discusses successful clinical translation cases exemplified by poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors, along with current challenges and future directions.
sources.full_text_excerpt: Introduction Synthetic lethality (SL) is a genetic interaction phenomenon in which cells survive when either of two genes is individually mutated, knocked down, or inhibited but die when both genes are simultaneously disrupted. This concept originated from genetic research in model organisms, which focused on revealing redundancy and complementarity among gene functions [ 1 ]. In cancer therapy, synthetic lethality strategies achieve precise targeting of cancer cells by disrupting synergistic survival pathways dependent on specific genetic defects (such as inactivated tumor suppressor genes or activated oncogenes) while maximally sparing normal cells. In recent years, advances in functional genomics and high-throughput screening technologies have transformed synthetic lethality from a fundamental genetic concept into a promising cancer treatment paradigm [ 2 ].  The concept of synthetic lethality originated from genetic studies in the early 20th century, gradually developing from observations in fruit fly hybrid experiments into a core theory for understanding genetic redundancy and complementation [ 3 ]. In the 21st century, research revealed that tumor cells with breast cancer susceptibility gene 1/2 (BRCA1/2) mutations are sensitive to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors because of defects in homologous recombination repair, providing the first successful example of clinical translation utilizing the SL strategy [ 4 ].  The core of the synthetic lethality strategy lies in exploiting tumor-specific genetic defects (such as the loss of tumor suppressor gene function or aberrant activation of oncogenes) to create targetable “vulnerabilities,” known as “non-oncogene addiction,” thereby achieving precise killing of cancer cells [ 5 ]. For example, tumors with BRCA1/2 mutations are highly dependent on PARP-mediated repair pathways because defects in homologous recombination repair, and inhibiting these pathways can lead to the accumulation of DNA damage and cell death. TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) kinase in KRAS-mutant tumors and myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) in MYC-driven tumors have also been identified as synthetic lethal targets. Epigenetic regulators, such as the stability of chromodomain helicase DNA binding protein 1 (CHD1) in the context of phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) loss and the dependence on DDB1 and CUL4 associated factor 5 (DCAF5) in SWI/SNF related, matrix associated, actin dependent regulator of chromatin, subfamily b, member 1 (SMARCB1)-mutant tumors, further highlight the complexity and diversity of synthetic lethal networks [ 6 ]. The theoretical advantage of this strategy is the potential for a clear therapeutic window, wherein the drug selectively kills cancer cells with specific genetic alterations while sparing normal cells. In practice, however, achieving this selectivity is often limited by tumor heterogeneity, adaptive resistance, and on target toxicity [ 7 ]. For instance, compared with traditional chemotherapy, the use of PARP inhibitors in patients with BRCA1/2 mutations significantly extends progression-free survival and results in lower toxicity. In addition, synthetic lethality can be used to target mutations traditionally considered “undruggable” (such as KRAS or tumor protein p53 (TP53)), thereby expanding the range of targets for anticancer drugs [ 8 ]. Successfully translating synthetic lethal interactions requires meeting several conditions: a clear therapeutic window, highly penetrant biomarkers, pharmacological feasibility, and the ability to adapt to tumor heterogeneity. Early studies have shown that BRCA-mutant cells are highly sensitive to PARP inhibition, with sustained and profound sensitivity, supporting clinical translation. Combining functional biomarkers (such as RAD51 recombinase (RAD51) foci formation assays) with genomic scar analysis can further improve the accuracy of patient selection and therapeutic benefit [ 9 ].  Molecular mechanisms of synthetic lethality DNA damage repair pathways DNA damage repair pathways are central to maintaining genomic stability, and their functional defects represent hallmarks of tumorigenesis. Moreover, these defects create targetable vulnerabilities that have been most extensively exploited in synthetic lethality. The intricate network formed by the homologous recombination repair pathway and PARP family proteins exemplifies the current understanding of synthetic lethality mechanisms. Core role and mechanism of the BRCA‒PARP axis The BRCA‒PARP axis represents the first successful translation of the synthetic lethality theory into cancer therapy. Its core mechanism lies in simultaneously disrupting two fundamental repair pathways for single-strand breaks (SSBs) and double-strand breaks (DSBs). In normal cells, poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase, particularly its canonical isoform PARP1 acts as a DNA damage sensor, rapidly recognizing and binding to single-strand breaks (SSBs). It catalyzes the synthesis of poly(ADP-ribose) chains, recruiting repair proteins such as X-ray repair cross complementing 1 (XRCC1) to efficiently repair SSBs. Additionally, PARP1 plays a crucial role in replication fork stabilization. When cells with intact homologous recombination repair (HRR) function are subjected to PARP inhibition, they can still survive by accurately repairing DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) that evolve during DNA replication because of unrepaired single-strand breaks (SSBs) via the HRR pathway. However, in tumor cells harboring pathogenic BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, homologous recombination repair is lost. In such cases, PARP inhibitors disrupt both repair pathways simultaneously by inhibiting PARP catalytic activity and blocking SSB repair; moreover, clinical drugs such as olaparib and talazoparib “trap” PARP1 at DNA damage sites [ 10 ]. This “PARP‒DNA complex” itself becomes a potent cytotoxic insult, impeding DNA replication and causing replication fork collapse, which in turn generates numerous double-strand breaks (DSBs). In the context of HRR deficiency, cells must rely on error-prone alternative pathways, such as alternative end joining, to repair these DSBs, ultimately leading to dramatic increases in genomic instability and cell death. Research on PARP inhibitor resistance mechanisms provides compelling genetic evidence for this model. Genome-wide and high-density CRISPR-Cas9 screening studies have revealed that, in addition to classic BRCA1/2 reversion mutations or deletions in HRR-related genes such as p53-binding protein 1 (53BP1) and REV7 homolog, DNA polymerase zeta accessory subunit (REV7), PARP1 gene mutations conferring resistance were also detected in PARP inhibitor-resistant cells [ 11 ]. These mutations span the DNA-binding zinc finger domain, regulatory domains, and even the catalytic domain. Their common feature is a significant impairment of the ability of PARP1 to be “trapped” on DNA by inhibitors rather than directly affecting its catalytic activity toward NAD⁺ [ 12 ]. This finding directly demonstrates that “PARP trapping” is the key mechanism mediating its cytotoxicity rather than simple catalytic inhibition. The R591C mutation causing loss of PARP1 trapping function was identified even in the tumor of an ovarian cancer patient with primary resistance to olaparib, further confirming the importance of this mechanism in clinical resistance (Fig.  1 ). Fig. 1 Mechanistic model of synthetic lethality between BRCA1/2 and PARP, and major resistance mechanisms.  A  In homologous recombination (HR)-proficient cells, PARP inhibitors bind to PARP1 and cause trapping on single-strand breaks (SSBs). Replication-associated double-strand breaks (DSBs) can still be accurately repaired by intact HR, allowing cell survival with limited cytotoxicity.  B  In BRCA1/2-deficient tumor cells, HR is impaired. PARP inhibition blocks SSB repair and “traps” PARP1 on DNA, leading to replication fork collapse and extensive DSB accumulation. In the absence of HR, cells rely on error-prone alternative end-joining pathways, resulting in catastrophic genomic instability and cell death—this constitutes the classical synthetic lethal interaction between BRCA1/2 loss and PARP inhibition.  C  Restoration of HR represents a major acquired resistance mechanism. Secondary BRCA1/2 reversion mutations or loss of 53BP1/Shieldin components partially restore DNA end resection and HR activity, allowing repair of PARP inhibitor-induced DSBs and conferring drug resistance.  D  PARP1 mutations that disrupt DNA binding or trapping (e.g., mutations in the zinc finger or R591C) reduce formation of toxic PARP1-DNA complexes without fully abolishing catalytic activity, thereby diminishing PARP inhibitor cytotoxicity and leading to clinical resistance HRR-related gene defects and PARP inhibitor sensitivity The “BRCAness” concept has significantly expanded the application prospects of PARP inhibitors beyond germline BRCA1/2 mutations. It refers to tumors that exhibit homologous recombination repair deficiency (HRD) through other mechanisms. As detailed in Section " Core role and mechanism of the BRCA‒PARP axis ", PARP inhibitors exert their synthetic lethal effect by trapping PARP1 on DNA in HR-deficient cells. Beyond BRCA1/2, the HRR pathway involves numerous genes, including partner and localizer of BRCA2 (PALB2), ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM), A ™  and Rad3-related (ATR), checkpoint kinase 2 (CHEK2), RAD51 and its paralogs, and genes in the Fanconi anemia pathway [ 13 ,  14 ], mutations that can also confer sensitivity to PARP inhibitors. Germline or somatic mutations in these genes impair homologous recombination repair (HRR) function to varying degrees, conferring cellular sensitivity to PARP inhibitors. For example, in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, deletions in genes such as A ™  and BRCA2 have been demonstrated to correlate with the clinical response to PARP inhibitors. Moreover, functional assessment of the HRR status is crucial for predicting PARP inhibitor sensitivity. Genomic scar analysis can retrospectively determine whether a tumor harbors HR defects by identifying characteristic mutation patterns such as large-scale state transitions. However, this approach fails to reflect the real-time functional status of the HRR at the time of treatment [ 15 ]. Therefore, functional biomarkers, such as the ability of RAD51 to form foci in the nucleus following DNA damage induction, as detected by immunofluorescence, have been shown to provide a more direct and dynamic reflection of HRR capacity [ 16 ]. These biomarkers can identify tumors sensitive to PARP inhibitors despite the absence of HRR gene mutations detected by conventional genetic testing. Notably, HRR defects are not the sole source of PARP-captured damage. Studies have revealed that ribonuclease H2 (RNase H2) deficiency leads to substantial accumulation of embedded ribonucleotides within the genome [ 17 ]. These ribonucleotides can be cleaved by topoisomerase I, generating numerous DNA single-strand breaks that subsequently serve as “substrates” captured by PARP. Consequently, RNase H2-deficient cells exhibit heightened sensitivity to PARP inhibitors. This repair vulnerability, termed ribonucleotide excision repair (RER) defects, arises from the inability to remove misincorporated ribonucleotides from DNA. Given that the ribonuclease H2 subunit B (RNASEH2B) gene is frequently lost because of 13q14 deletions in chronic lymphocytic leukemia and metastatic prostate cancer, this discovery provides novel theoretical support for the application of PARP inhibitors to tumors with intact HRR function but ribonucleotide excision repair (RER) defects. Reverse synthetic lethality between POLQ and HRR Further investigation of HR-deficient tumors revealed a novel synthetic lethal relationship beyond the BRCA‒PARP paradigm, namely, an inverse synthetic lethality between the HRR pathway and DNA polymerase θ. Classic synthetic lethal HRR-BER/SSBR: Within the BRCA‒PARP axis, HRR and BER/SSBR are two parallel, functionally complementary pathways primarily responsible for DSB and SSB repair, respectively. When HRR is inactivated, cells become highly sensitive to disruption of BER/SSBR (via PARP inhibition). This effect demonstrates synthetic lethality targeting parallel complementary pathways. Reverse synthetic lethal HRR-TMEJ: DNA polymerase θ (POLQ) serves as the central effector of theta-mediated end-joining (TMEJ), an error-prone pathway for DNA double-strand break repair that operates independently of homologous recombination [ 18 ]. In HR-proficient cells, POLQ expression is low, and its inhibition does not compromise viability; indeed, suppressing POLQ can even increase HR efficiency by promoting RAD51 nuclear filament assembly [ 19 ]. This finding indicates that the POLQ-mediated TMEJ pathway is ordinarily suppressed when HR is functional. However, in HR-deficient tumors—such as many high-grade serous ovarian cancers—POLQ expression is significantly upregulated and is essential for survival. Mechanistically, POLQ performs a dual function: its C-terminal polymerase domain executes TMEJ, while its N-terminal helicase-like domain contains a RAD51-binding motif that actively disrupts RAD51-ssDNA nucleofilament assembly, thereby antagonizing any residual HR activity that could be toxic to HR-deficient cells. By providing a critical alternative repair pathway (TMEJ) while simultaneously suppressing residual HR, POLQ becomes indispensable for the survival of HR-deficient tumors. Consequently, pharmacological inhibition of POLQ selectively kills HR-deficient cells, establishing a robust synthetic lethal interaction with significant therapeutic potential. This “reverse” synthetic lethality contrasts with the classic parallel pathway relationship: in HR-proficient cells, POLQ inhibition is harmless and may even promote more precise HR repair; conversely, HR-deficient tumors become critically dependent on POLQ for survival. Genetic evidence supports this dependency, as Fancd2⁻/⁻Polq⁻/⁻ double knockout causes embryonic lethality in mice, and POLQ knockdown in HR-deficient xenograft models significantly enhances sensitivity to PARP inhibitors. Collectively, synthetic lethal networks in DNA damage repair extend far beyond the BRCA‒PARP axis. These discoveries greatly expand the understanding of synthetic lethal molecular mechanisms, from defects in the HRR caused by BRCAness to novel PARP-captured damage sources revealed by RNase H2 deficiency and the intricate interplay between HRR and POLQ. These findings provide a robust foundation for precisely identifying beneficial populations and developing next-generation targeted therapeutics (Table  1 ). Table 1 DNA Damage Repair-Related Synthetic Lethal Therapies Key Factor or Pathway Agent Major Mechanism Tumor Type Year and Reference HRR-POLQ (Reverse Synthetic Lethality) POLQ inhibitor (preclinical) HR-deficient tumors depend on POLQ for error-prone repair; inhibition induces genomic instability High-grade serous ovarian cancer 2015 [ 18 ] RNase H2-PARP Axis PARP inhibitors (olaparib) RNase H2 deficiency leads to ribonucleotide accumulation and SSBs; PARP trapping amplifies DNA damage Chronic lymphocytic leukemia, metastatic prostate cancer 2018 [ 17 ] ATM-ATR Axis ATR inhibitors (ceralasertib) ATM deficiency enhances dependence on ATR; inhibition disrupts replication stress response Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2016 [ 91 ] LIG1/PARP (Non-HRR Deficiency) PARP inhibitors (talazoparib) LIG1 deletion impairs DNA repair; PARP inhibition blocks compensatory SSB repair Solid tumors with LIG1 loss 2021 [ 2 ] EME1/PARP (Non-HRR Deficiency) PARP inhibitors (rucaparib) EME1 deficiency interacts synthetically with PARP inhibition via disrupted DNA repair Multiple solid tumors 2021 [ 2 ] Synthetic lethal effects on cell cycle checkpoint regulation Cell cycle checkpoints are core regulatory mechanisms for maintaining genomic integrity. The TP53-regulated G1/S checkpoint and the ATR-CHK1-WEE1 pathway-regulated G2/M checkpoint form a dual safeguard. However, in most cancers, frequent TP53 inactivation leads to loss of G1/S checkpoint function, forcing cancer cells to become highly dependent on the G2/M checkpoint to cope with replication stress. This dependency provides a strong rationale for targeting A ™  and Rad3-related (ATR), checkpoint kinase 1 (CHK1), or WEE1 G2 checkpoint kinase (WEE1) in TP53-deficient tumors, as detailed in this section. This section systematically elucidates the core mechanisms linking TP53 inactivation to G2/M checkpoint dependency, with a focus on translational advances in WEE1 and CHK1 inhibitor-based synthetic lethal strategies (Fig.  2 ). Fig. 2 TP53 inactivation creates a G2/M checkpoint dependency that underlies synthetic lethality with ATR-CHK1-WEE1 inhibition. In TP53 wild-type cells (left), DNA damage activates p53 and its downstream effector p21, enforcing a robust G1/S checkpoint that allows damage repair before DNA replication. In parallel, replication stress activates the ATR-CHK1-WEE1 axis, which phosphorylates and inactivates CDK1, thereby inducing a G2/M checkpoint and preventing mitotic entry with damaged DNA.In TP53-deficient cancer cells (right), the G1/S checkpoint is lost, and cells proceed through S phase with unrepaired damage, leading to elevated replication stress and DNA breaks. To survive, these cells become highly dependent on the ATR-CHK1-WEE1-mediated G2/M checkpoint (“single checkpoint dependency”). Pharmacologic inhibition of ATR, CHK1, or WEE1 abolishes the G2/M checkpoint, forcing TP53-deficient cells with extensive DNA damage into premature mitosis. This results in mitotic catastrophe (chromosomal fragmentation, micronuclei) and selective cell death, establishing a synthetic lethal relationship between TP53 loss and ATR/CHK1/WEE1 inhibition Core mechanism: TP53 inactivation and G2/M checkpoint dependency As the “guardian of the genome,” TP53 plays a central role in the G1/S checkpoint by responding to DNA damage through transcriptional activation of effector proteins such as cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1 A (p21), thereby arresting cell cycle progression to facilitate repair [ 20 ]. Loss of TP53 function (via mutation or deletion) is among the most common genetic events in cancer, occurring in approximately 50% of all tumors. This process directly results in defective G1/S checkpoint function, preventing cells from effectively arresting and repairing damage before DNA replication. Consequently, extensive DNA breaks and replication stress accumulate. To maintain survival, TP53-deficient cancer cells compensate by upregulating G2/M checkpoint activity. This adaptive dependency forms the molecular basis for synthetic lethality. The G2/M checkpoint is precisely regulated by the ATR-CHK1-WEE1 signaling cascade [ 21 ]. Upon DNA damage or replication stress, ATR is activated and phosphorylates CHK1. CHK1 then inhibits cell division cycle 25 (CDC25) phosphatase activity and activates WEE1 kinase activity, promoting the phosphorylation of cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1) at Tyr15. This process blocks the activation of the CDK1-cyclin B complex, arresting cells in the G2 phase. Studies have indicated significantly elevated endogenous replication stress levels in TP53-deficient cells, further underscoring the dependence on the ATR-CHK1-WEE1 pathway. Studies have also shown that endogenous replication stress levels are significantly increased in TP53-deficient cells, making them more dependent on the ATR-CHK1-WEE1 pathway. For example, under ATR inhibition, compared with wild-type cells, TP53-deficient mouse embryonic fibroblasts exhibit increased levels of replication stress, as evidenced by the subsequent expression of DNA damage markers (pannuclear γH2AX staining, which is indicative of replication fork collapse) and increased apoptosis [ 22 ,  23 ]. In the context of oncogenes such as cyclin E1 (CCNE1) being overexpressed and exacerbating replication stress, TP53 inactivation further amplifies this dependency [ 24 ,  25 ]. ATR inhibitors synergistically induce p53-independent apoptosis, confirming the synergistic lethal interaction of TP53 inactivation and ATR inhibition. In addition to ATRs, the downstream effectors CHK1 and WEE1 also exhibit synthetic lethality with TP53 deficiency [ 26 ]. Mechanistically, inhibiting CHK1 or WEE1 abolishes the G2/M checkpoint, forcing cells with unrepaired DNA damage to prematurely enter mitosis and undergo mitotic catastrophe (e.g., micronucleus formation and chromosomal fragmentation). Notably, this synthetic lethality exhibits pathway specificity: while PI3K/mTOR inhibitors target growth factor signaling and cannot directly impinge on the G2/M checkpoint, even at their maximum tolerated clinical doses (e.g., alpelisib 400 mg daily; bimiralisib 80–140 mg daily) [ 27 ,  28 ], these agents fail to induce the selective lethality observed with ATR/CHK1/WEE1 inhibition in TP53-deficient cells, underscoring that this vulnerability is uniquely linked to G2/M checkpoint dependency. Preclinical models further validated that in TP53-deficient ovarian, colorectal, and pancreatic xenografts, WEE1 or CHK1 inhibitors combined with DNA-damaging agents (e.g., gemcitabine and cisplatin) significantly suppressed tumor growth but had minimal effects on TP53 wild-type models. In summary, TP53 inactivation creates unique synthetic lethal vulnerability by disrupting the G1/S checkpoint and increasing the dependence on the G2/M checkpoint. Targeting the ATR-CHK1-WEE1 axis not only selectively eliminates TP53-deficient cancer cells but also provides an indirect targeting strategy for traditionally “undruggable” TP53 mutations [ 29 ].  Synthetic lethal effects of WEE1 inhibitors WEE1 kinase serves as a core negative regulator of the G2/M checkpoint by maintaining CDK1-Tyr15 in an inactivated state through phosphorylation, thereby preventing progression to mitosis [ 30 ]. In TP53-deficient cancer cells, WEE1 expression is frequently upregulated to counteract heightened replication stress and DNA damage burdens, making WEE1 an ideal target for synthetic lethality [ 31 ].  WEE1 inhibitors (e.g., AZD1775, formerly MK1775) antagonize WEE1 kinase activity, leading to premature CDK1 activation and abolishing the G2/M checkpoint [ 32 ]. In TP53-deficient cells, this action induces synthetic lethality; cells fail to arrest in the G1 phase and lose the G2 repair window, ultimately succumbing to mitotic catastrophe. Studies have demonstrated that AZD1775 effectively inhibits WEE1 at nanomolar concentrations (IC₅₀=5 nM) and induces selective apoptosis in TP53-deficient cervical, colorectal, and pancreatic cancer cell lines, with apoptosis rates 3–5 times greater than those in TP53 wild-type cells [ 33 ]. Furthermore, combining AZD1775 with DNA-damaging agents (e.g., cisplatin and gemcitabine) further amplifies the synthetic lethality effect. In TP53-deficient ovarian cancer xenograft models, the combination of AZD1775 and carboplatin resulted in tumor inhibition rates of 70%-80%, whereas the rates were only 20%-30% with carboplatin alone. AZD1775 is the most advanced WEE1 inhibitor to date. As of 2016, 34 clinical trials have evaluated its safety and efficacy in combination with DNA-damaging agents. Phase I studies have demonstrated that in patients with advanced solid tumors, the objective response rate to AZD1775 combined with cisplatin reached 30% in the TP53-deficient subgroup, which was significantly higher than that in the overall population (15%) [ 34 ]. Dose-limiting toxicities primarily included myelosuppression and supraventricular tachycardia, although they were generally manageable. Notably, a Phase I study ( NCT01748825 ) revealed partial responses in patients with BRCA1 mutations, suggesting that WEE1 inhibition may result in synergistic synthetic lethality with homologous recombination repair defects [ 35 ].  However, the clinical application of WEE1 inhibitors faces several challenges [ 36 ], including the off-target effects of AZD1775 (such as inhibition of YES1 and SYK), insufficient blood‒brain barrier penetration, which limits its use in brain tumors, and the lack of precise biomarkers for patient selection. Future directions include developing highly selective WEE1 inhibitors (e.g., CJM061, whose single-agent toxicity is 50% lower than that of AZD1775), optimizing dosing regimens to increase intracerebral concentrations, and integrating functional biomarkers (e.g., replication stress scores) for precise identification of beneficial populations. Clinical translation of CHK1 inhibitors As a downstream effector of ATR, CHK1 plays a central role in the DNA damage response and replication fork stability. Its inhibition disrupts the G2/M checkpoint and induces synthetic lethality under high replication stress, particularly in TP53-deficient tumors. CHK1 inhibitors (e.g., LY2606368) block CHK1-mediated phosphorylation of cell division cycle 25 C (CDC25C), leading to sustained CDK1 activation and forcing cells to enter mitosis with DNA damage [ 37 ]. In TP53-deficient cells, the absence of the G1/S checkpoint renders CHK1 inhibition lethal, triggering a “replication catastrophe” characterized by replication fork collapse, accumulation of DNA double-strand breaks, and elevated phosphorylated H2A histone family member X (pH2A.X) levels. Nonclinical studies have demonstrated that LY2606368 has an IC₅₀ of 1 nM for CHK1 inhibition in cell-free assays and induces tumor regression via pCHK1 suppression in a Calu-6 xenograft model [ 38 ]. PK/PD modeling predicted a minimal tumor response at an average pCHK1 inhibition rate of 49.7% within 72 h, with a maximal response achieved at 70.5%. A Phase I study of LY2606368 demonstrated objective responses for the first time when a CHK1/CHK2 inhibitor was used as monotherapy. Among 45 patients with advanced cancer, two patients with squamous cell carcinoma achieved a partial response (PR), and 15 patients experienced stable disease (SD), with response durations ranging from 1.2 to 7.2 months. Notably, all the responders had SCC (anal SCC and head/neck SCC), suggesting that tumor types with higher replication stress levels exhibit greater sensitivity to CHK1 inhibition. Mechanistically, SCC often involves oncogene activation (e.g., CCND1 amplification) and DNA repair defects, leading to elevated endogenous replication stress and increased dependence on the CHK1 checkpoint. In terms of safety, the primary dose-limiting toxicity of LY2606368 was transient Grade 4 neutropenia (73.3% incidence), which was short-lived (typically < 5 days) and did not result in treatment-related death. This toxicity stems from the role of CHK1 in hematopoietic stem cell cycle regulation, but its reversibility highlights the selectivity of synthetic lethality as normal cells recover through compensatory mechanisms while TP53-deficient cancer cells undergo apoptosis. However, the clinical translation of CHK1 inhibitors remains challenging. First, reliable PD biomarkers are lacking. Follicular pH2A.X is not significantly correlated with tumor response, and circulating tumor cell counts were insufficient for analysis. Second, the association of TP53 status with treatment efficacy was inconsistent. However, some TP53 wild-type SCC patients achieved disease stabilization, suggesting potential alternative predictors (e.g., replication stress score or HR deficiency). Future research should focus on developing combination biomarkers (e.g., pCHK1/pH2A.X levels in tumor biopsies) and exploring combination strategies of LY2606368 with DNA-damaging agents (e.g., gemcitabine) to further amplify synergistic lethal effects. Synthetic lethality in cell cycle checkpoint regulation represents a key paradigm for precision oncology. TP53 inactivation creates “G2/M checkpoint-dependent” vulnerability, offering an ideal window for targeting the ATR-CHK1-WEE1 axis. Preclinical and early clinical data on WEE1 and CHK1 inhibitors have thoroughly validated the feasibility and selectivity of this strategy, demonstrating particularly significant efficacy in TP53-deficient or high-replication-stress tumors. Future efforts to optimize inhibitor selectivity, develop novel biomarkers, and explore rational combination regimens hold promise for expanding the application scope of synthetic lethal strategies, offering more precise therapeutic options for refractory cancers [ 39 ].  Synthetic lethal effects on metabolic pathways Metabolic reprogramming is a core feature of tumor cells. It not only rapidly supplies biosynthetic precursors but also directly influences epigenetic regulation and genomic stability by altering metabolite levels, thereby generating context-specific metabolic dependencies that can be therapeutically targeted [ 39 ]. Metabolism-related synthetic lethality primarily arises from two mechanisms: the abnormal dependence of cancer cells on specific metabolic pathways and DNA repair defects caused by the accumulation of oncogenic metabolites. These mechanisms collectively form the theoretical basis for metabolism-directed synthetic lethality strategies. Core mechanism: synthetic lethal opportunities generated by metabolic reprogramming Metabolic reprogramming in tumor cells involves adaptive alterations across glycolysis, amino acid metabolism, lipid synthesis, and mitochondrial function. While these alterations promote tumor growth, they also create specific metabolic dependencies—the phenomenon known as “nononcogene addiction”. When key metabolic enzymes undergo mutation or abnormal expression, tumor cells must upregulate alternative or bypass pathways to maintain viability. This adaptive dependency becomes an ideal target for synthetic lethality interventions. For example, in colorectal cancer, APC loss upregulates the expression of tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO2) by continuously activating the β-catenin signaling pathway, promoting the breakdown of tryptophan into kynurenine. The latter facilitates tumor proliferation and inhibits T-cell function through aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) signaling, thereby remodeling the immunosuppressive microenvironment [ 40 ]. TDO2 inhibitors can selectively induce apoptosis in APC-mutant models, confirming the synthetic lethality relationship between APC loss and TDO2 inhibition [ 41 ].  Another significant example is MYC-driven metabolic vulnerability [ 42 ]. Overexpression of the MYC oncogene promotes cell proliferation and metabolic reprogramming across multiple tumors while revealing specific metabolic dependencies. Studies indicate that MYC-overexpressing tumors exhibit high sensitivity to the inhibition of mitochondrial complex I [ 43 ]. Mechanistically, MYC drives glutamine metabolism and oxidative phosphorylation, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels [ 44 ]. The inhibition of complex I further exacerbates oxidative stress beyond the tolerance threshold of cancer cells, inducing nonapoptotic cell death, such as ferroptosis. This mechanism offers novel therapeutic approaches for MYC-driven tumors, particularly those with traditionally challenging MYC overexpression. Furthermore, nucleotide metabolism presents abundant synthetic lethal opportunities [ 45 ]. In tumors lacking methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (MTAP), cells exhibit heightened sensitivity to protein arginine methyltransferase 5 (PRMT5) inhibition because of accumulated 5’-deoxy-5’-methylthioadenosine (MTA). Mechanistically, MTA competitively inhibits PRMT5 activity, forcing MTAP-deficient cells to upregulate PRMT5 expression for survival and inhibitors then synergistically induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. This synthetic lethal relationship has been validated across multiple MTAP-deficient tumor models, including glioma, pancreatic cancer, and lung cancer. ME2-ME3 axis paradigm: synthetic lethal network of metabolic enzyme cross-regulation The metabolic axis formed by malate decarboxylase 2 (malic enzyme 2 (ME2)) and malate decarboxylase 3 (malic enzyme 3 (ME3)) provides a classic example of metabolic synthetic lethality [ 46 ]. ME2 and ME3 catalyze the oxidative decarboxylation of malate to pyruvate, simultaneously generating NADH or NADPH, thereby linking the tricarboxylic acid cycle to the mitochondrial electron transport chain. In normal cells, ME2 and ME3 exhibit functional redundancy, together maintaining cellular redox homeostasis and biosynthetic demands. Research has revealed that in ME2-deficient tumor cells, the mitochondrial NADH/NADPH balance is disrupted, forcing cells to rely on ME3 to maintain metabolic homeostasis. In this state, inhibiting ME3 induces severe oxidative stress and an energy crisis, selectively killing ME2-deficient cells. Mechanistically, ME2 deficiency causes mitochondrial malate accumulation and impaired NAD+ regeneration, disrupting TCA cycle flux. Simultaneous ME3 inhibition further blocks malate metabolism, leading to mitochondrial collapse. This synthetic lethal relationship was validated in glioblastoma and lung cancer models, providing a specific therapeutic target for ME2-low tumors. Notably, the synthetic lethality of the ME2-ME3 axis is significantly influenced by tissue type and genetic background. In KRAS-mutant lung cancer, ME2 expression is typically downregulated, increasing the sensitivity of cells to ME3 inhibition. Conversely, the dependence of BRAF-mutant melanoma on the ME2-ME3 axis is weaker. This context-dependent behavior reflects the complexity of metabolic synthetic lethality, suggesting the need for patient stratification on the basis of specific molecular tumor characteristics. From a translational medicine perspective, strategies targeting the ME2‒ME3 axis face challenges, primarily because of the current lack of highly selective ME3 inhibitors. However, on the basis of this synthetic lethality principle, researchers are exploring indirect intervention strategies, such as amplifying metabolic stress in ME2-deficient cells by modulating mitochondrial membrane potential or reactive oxygen species levels, providing alternative pathways for clinical translation. Cross-Talk between metabolic abnormalities and genomic stability The cross-talk between metabolic abnormalities and genomic stability provides another critical dimension for synthetic lethality [ 47 ]. The accumulation of oncogenic metabolites can directly or indirectly disrupt DNA repair mechanisms, creating opportunities for synthetic lethality when combined with DNA damage response inhibitors. The accumulation of 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) caused by isocitrate dehydrogenase 1/2 (IDH1/2) mutations exemplifies this mechanism [ 48 ]. As a structural analog of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG), 2-HG competitively inhibits multiple α-KG-dependent dioxygenases, including histone demethylases and DNA demethylases. Research has indicated that 2-HG disrupts chromatin signaling at DNA damage sites by inhibiting the histone demethylase lysine demethylase 4B (KDM4B), leading to an abnormal increase in the level of histone H3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3). Specifically, the transient peak of H3K9me3 following DNA double-strand breaks in normal cells is essential for recruiting the Tip60 (KAT5, lysine acetyltransferase 5)-A ™  complex and initiating homologous recombination repair. In IDH-mutated cells, however, the baseline H3K9me3 level is abnormally elevated, masking the damage-induced signaling peak. This leads to impaired A ™  recruitment, defective DNA end excision, and reduced RAD51 foci formation. This IDH mutation-induced HR defect renders tumor cells highly sensitive to PARP inhibitors. Studies have demonstrated that compared with wild-type cells, IDH1-mutated glioblastoma cells and fumarate hydratase (FH)-deficient renal carcinoma cells exhibit 3- to 5-fold increased sensitivity to PARP inhibitors. Supplementing α-KG or overexpressing KDM4B reversed abnormal H3K9me3 patterns and repaired defects, restoring sensitivity to PARP inhibitors and confirming the causal relationship between metabolic abnormalities and DNA repair defects. Similar mechanisms have been observed in tumors with succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) and fumarate hydratase (FH) defects [ 49 ]. SDH mutations cause succinate accumulation, inhibiting the expression of multiple α-KG-dependent histone and DNA demethylases; [ 50 ] FH mutations lead to the accumulation of fumarate, which not only suppresses α-KG-dependent enzymes but also directly alkylates DNA and proteins, inducing DNA damage [ 51 ]. These metabolic abnormalities collectively increase sensitivity to PARP inhibitors, providing a theoretical basis for precision therapy in related tumors. From a clinical translation perspective, metabolism-targeted synthetic lethal strategies hold significant value [ 52 ]. First, metabolic abnormalities are often driven by specific mutations, providing ideal biomarkers. Second, metabolic states can be noninvasively monitored by imaging or metabolomics, facilitating treatment response assessment. Finally, drugs targeting metabolic abnormalities may exhibit synergistic effects when combined with traditional DNA-damaging agents, enhancing therapeutic efficacy while reducing toxicity. However, metabolic synthetic lethality strategies also face challenges. Tumor metabolism is highly plastic and heterogeneous, potentially leading to resistance through metabolic reprogramming. Additionally, metabolic pathways perform critical functions in normal tissues, necessitating careful evaluation of therapeutic windows. Future research should integrate multiomics approaches to systematically decipher the interactions between metabolic networks and genetic backgrounds and identify patient populations most likely to benefit from metabolism-directed synthetic lethality strategies. In addition to the oncometabolite-mediated mechanisms discussed above, a conceptually distinct form of metabolic synthetic lethality has recently emerged through the paradigm of synthetic dosage lethality (SDL). Unlike classical synthetic lethality, which involves loss-of-function mutations in both genes, SDL occurs when overexpression of a gene (typically an oncogene) results in a dependency on another gene that is not essential in normal cells. This concept is particularly relevant for targeting oncogenes that are difficult to inhibit directly, such as Polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1). PLK1 is overexpressed in a wide range of cancers and drives chromosomal instability, yet direct PLK1 inhibitors have shown limited clinical success because of off-target toxicity and narrow therapeutic windows [ 53 ]. To overcome this challenge, a genome-wide SDL screen was performed to identify genes whose inhibition selectively kills PLK1-overexpressing cells. This approach identified IGF2BP2 as a critical SDL partner—a finding validated by both in vivo and in vitro CRISPR screens at single-cell resolution. Mechanistically, the loss of IGF2BP2 disrupts mitochondrial metabolism by downregulating PLK1 expression and suppressing the expression of oxidative phosphorylation genes, leading to impaired ATP production and the selective elimination of PLK1-overexpressing cancer cells. Pharmacological inhibition of IGF2BP2 confirmed this synthetic dosage lethal interaction, demonstrating that targeting metabolic vulnerability can circumvent the challenges associated with direct oncogene inhibition. This work established SDL as a powerful framework for identifying context-dependent metabolic dependencies in tumors driven by oncogene overexpression. This concept aligns with a broader emerging paradigm in which targeting metabolic vulnerabilities—whether through classical synthetic lethality or SDL—is increasingly recognized as a key strategy to overcome therapeutic resistance, particularly in the context of oncogene-driven metabolic reprogramming [ 54 ]. sources.title: The computational analysis of tumor cell sensitivity to supertarget deletion.
sources.abstract: Gene mutations and altered epigenetic regulation of gene expression are characteristic features of malignant neoplasms. Combinations of these abnormalities form molecular features of individual tumors. In the large-scale Dependency Map (DepMap) project, the broad panels of human tumor cell lines are being tested for sensitivity to single gene inactivation. Using DepMap data, we have previously identified a set of genes termed supertargets, the deletion of which significantly reduced the survival of cells of a particular tissue origin while minimally impairing the unrelated cell lines. In the present study, we determined the factors of viability (inhibition of proliferation or death) of cell lines in which the supertarget genes have been deleted. We found that, in 79 % of cases, the reduced survival may be caused by epigenetic changes of gene expression. In the remaining 21 % of cases, it is associated with altered gene structure. Three groups containing different types of gene expression alterations can be distinguished. In the first group, the reduced cell survival correlated with a higher expression of the supertarget gene (e. g., SOX10 and HNF1B). In the second group, a gene different from the deleted supertarget was overexpressed (gene pairs: FOXA1 and SPDEF, TP63 and SERPINB13, etc.). The third group was characterized by correlations between low expression of a certain gene and tumor cell sensitivity (e. g., FAM126A and FAM126B, SMARCA2 and SMARCA4). The genetic changes included GOF mutations (KRAS, BRAF genes, etc.), LOF mutations (STAG1, SMARCA2 genes, etc.), gene fusions (BCR-ABL1, PAX3-FOXO1, etc.), and amplification (CPM, BEST3, etc.). Therefore, many different molecular mechanisms act as predictors of tumor cell response to inhibition of supertarget genes.
